concepts.statement: Let ρ(x) be an integrable function representing the radial density of a disk of radius r. Breaking the disk into thin washers of area about 2πxᵢ*Δx, the mass of the disk is the integral of 2πxρ(x) from 0 to r.

concepts.name: Work
concepts.statement: Work is the amount of energy it takes to move an object; when a force is constant, work is the product of force and distance. If a variable force F(x) moves an object in a positive direction along the x-axis from point a to point b, the work done on the object is the integral of F(x) from a to b.

concepts.name: Hooke’s law
concepts.statement: The force required to compress or stretch a spring from its equilibrium position is proportional to the distance it has been compressed or stretched: F(x) = kx, where the spring constant k depends on the physical characteristics of the spring and is always positive.

concepts.name: Solving pumping problems
concepts.statement: Sketch the tank and select a frame of reference; calculate the volume of a representative layer of water and multiply it by the weight-density of water to get the force; multiply by the distance the layer must be lifted to estimate the work for that layer; sum over the layers, a Riemann sum, and take the limit to get the work as an integral.

concepts.name: Hydrostatic pressure
concepts.statement: Hydrostatic pressure is the pressure exerted by water on a submerged object: on a plate of area A submerged horizontally at depth s, the force is the weight ρAs of the water above it, and the pressure is p = F/A = ρs, where ρ is the weight density of water.

concepts.name: Pascal’s principle
concepts.statement: The pressure at a given depth in a liquid is the same in all directions, so it does not matter whether a plate is submerged horizontally or vertically.

concepts.name: Hydrostatic force on a plate
concepts.statement: For a thin plate submerged vertically in a liquid of weight density ρ, with the x-axis oriented vertically and downward positive, the top edge of the plate at x = a and the bottom at x = b, the depth s(x) and the width w(x) of the plate at x, the force on the plate is the integral of ρw(x)s(x) from a to b, the limit of the forces on thin horizontal strips each treated as at constant depth.

concepts.name: Finding hydrostatic force
concepts.statement: Sketch a picture and select an appropriate frame of reference; determine the depth and width functions s(x) and w(x); determine the weight-density of the liquid; and use the integral of ρw(x)s(x) to calculate the total force.

concepts.name: Moment
concepts.statement: If n masses are arranged on a number line, the moment of the system with respect to the origin is M = Σmᵢxᵢ; for a region in the plane bounded above by a function f(x) over [a, b], the moments of the region with respect to the x- and y-axes are Mₓ = ρ∫[f(x)]²/2 dx and M_y = ρ∫x f(x) dx.

concepts.name: Center of mass
concepts.statement: The center of mass of a system is the point at which the total mass of the system could be concentrated without changing the moment; loosely, its balancing point. For two masses on a number line it is the point where a fulcrum makes the system balance.

concepts.name: Center of mass of objects on a line
concepts.statement: Let m₁, m₂, …, mₙ be point masses placed on a number line at points x₁, x₂, …, xₙ and let m be the total mass of the system. The moment of the system with respect to the origin is M = Σmᵢxᵢ, and the center of mass of the system is x̄ = M/m.

concepts.name: Center of mass of objects in a plane
concepts.statement: Let m₁, m₂, …, mₙ be point masses located in the xy-plane at points (x₁, y₁), …, (xₙ, yₙ) and let m be the total mass. The moments of the system with respect to the x- and y-axes are Mₓ = Σmᵢyᵢ and M_y = Σmᵢxᵢ, and the center of mass is (x̄, ȳ) with x̄ = M_y/m and ȳ = Mₓ/m.

concepts.name: Lamina
concepts.statement: A lamina is a thin sheet of material, thin enough that, for mathematical purposes, it can be treated as if it is two-dimensional.

concepts.name: Centroid
concepts.statement: The centroid of a region is the geometric center of the region; if a lamina has constant density, its center of mass depends only on the shape of the corresponding planar region and corresponds to the centroid of that region.

concepts.name: Symmetry principle
concepts.statement: If a region R is symmetric about a line l, then the centroid of R lies on l.

concepts.name: Center of mass of a thin plate
concepts.statement: Let R be the region bounded above by the graph of a continuous function f(x), below by the x-axis and on the left and right by x = a and x = b, and let ρ be the density of the lamina. Its mass is m = ρ∫f(x)dx, its moments are Mₓ = ρ∫[f(x)]²/2 dx and M_y = ρ∫x f(x) dx, and its center of mass is x̄ = M_y/m, ȳ = Mₓ/m; the constant ρ cancels from the coordinates.

concepts.name: Center of mass of a lamina bounded by two functions
concepts.statement: Let R be the region bounded above by the graph of a continuous function f(x), below by the graph of a continuous function g(x), and on the left and right by x = a and x = b, and let ρ be the density of the lamina. Its mass is m = ρ∫[f(x) − g(x)]dx, its moments are Mₓ = ρ∫½([f(x)]² − [g(x)]²)dx and M_y = ρ∫x[f(x) − g(x)]dx, and its center of mass is x̄ = M_y/m, ȳ = Mₓ/m.

concepts.name: Theorem of Pappus for volume
concepts.statement: Let R be a region in the plane and let l be a line in the plane that does not intersect R. The volume of the solid of revolution formed by revolving R around l is equal to the area of R multiplied by the distance d traveled by the centroid of R.

concepts.name: Natural logarithm as an integral
concepts.statement: For x > 0, the natural logarithm function is defined by ln x = ∫₁ˣ (1/t) dt: for x > 1 it is the area under the curve y = 1/t from 1 to x, and for x < 1 the negative of the area from x to 1. It follows that ln 1 = 0 and that ln x is increasing for x > 0.

concepts.name: Continuity of the natural logarithm
concepts.statement: The function ln x is differentiable; therefore, it is continuous throughout its domain (0, ∞).

concepts.name: The number e as an area
concepts.statement: The number e is defined to be the real number such that ln e = 1: the area under the curve y = 1/t between t = 1 and t = e is 1. Its approximate value is 2.71828182846.

concepts.name: Exponential function as the inverse of the natural logarithm
concepts.statement: The natural logarithm is one-to-one, so it has an inverse function, exp x. For any real number x, eˣ is defined to be the number y for which ln y = ln(eˣ) = x; then eˣ = exp x for all x, e^{ln x} = x for x > 0 and ln(eˣ) = x for all x.

concepts.name: General exponential function in terms of e
concepts.statement: For any a > 0 and any real number x, aˣ is defined as e^{x ln a}, which defines aˣ rigorously for irrational x as well and lets the properties of exponents and logarithms hold for every real exponent.

concepts.name: Exponential growth model
concepts.statement: Systems that exhibit exponential growth increase according to the model y = y₀e^{kt}, where y₀ represents the initial state of the system and k > 0 is a constant, the growth constant. The rate of growth is proportional to the current value: y′ = ky, a differential equation.

concepts.name: Doubling time
concepts.statement: If a quantity grows exponentially, the doubling time is the amount of time it takes the quantity to double, which stays the same whatever the starting size; it is (ln 2)/k.

concepts.name: Exponential decay model
concepts.statement: Systems that exhibit exponential decay behave according to the model y = y₀e^{−kt}, where y₀ represents the initial state and k > 0 is a constant, the decay constant; then y′ = −ky.

concepts.name: Newton’s law of cooling
concepts.statement: An object cools at a rate proportional to the difference between its temperature and the temperature of its surroundings, T′ = −k(T − Tₐ); with y = T − Tₐ this is exponential decay, so T = (T₀ − Tₐ)e^{−kt} + Tₐ, where T₀ is the initial temperature.

concepts.name: Half-life
concepts.statement: If a quantity decays exponentially, the half-life is the amount of time it takes the quantity to be reduced by half; it is (ln 2)/k.

concepts.name: Derivatives of the hyperbolic functions
concepts.statement: From their definitions in terms of eˣ and e⁻ˣ, the hyperbolic functions differentiate as d/dx sinh x = cosh x, d/dx cosh x = sinh x, d/dx tanh x = sech² x, d/dx coth x = −csch² x, d/dx sech x = −sech x tanh x and d/dx csch x = −csch x coth x; unlike cos x, the derivative of cosh x carries no minus sign.

concepts.name: Integrals of the hyperbolic functions
concepts.statement: The differentiation formulas lead directly to ∫sinh u du = cosh u + C, ∫cosh u du = sinh u + C, ∫sech² u du = tanh u + C, ∫csch² u du = −coth u + C, ∫sech u tanh u du = −sech u + C and ∫csch u coth u du = −csch u + C.

concepts.name: Derivatives of the inverse hyperbolic functions
concepts.statement: By implicit differentiation and the identity cosh² y − sinh² y = 1, d/dx sinh⁻¹ x = 1/√(1 + x²), d/dx cosh⁻¹ x = 1/√(x² − 1), d/dx tanh⁻¹ x = d/dx coth⁻¹ x = 1/(1 − x²), d/dx sech⁻¹ x = −1/(x√(1 − x²)) and d/dx csch⁻¹ x = −1/(|x|√(1 + x²)).

concepts.name: Integrals involving the inverse hyperbolic functions
concepts.statement: ∫du/√(1 + u²) = sinh⁻¹ u + C; ∫du/√(u² − 1) = cosh⁻¹ u + C; ∫du/(1 − u²) is tanh⁻¹ u + C if |u| < 1 and coth⁻¹ u + C if |u| > 1, the antiderivative chosen by the domain; ∫du/(u√(1 − u²)) = −sech⁻¹|u| + C; ∫du/(u√(1 + u²)) = −csch⁻¹|u| + C.

concepts.name: Catenary
concepts.statement: A catenary is a curve in the shape of the function y = a cosh(x/a); a cable of uniform density suspended between two supports, with no load other than its own weight, assumes the shape of a catenary.

concepts.name: Integration by parts
concepts.statement: If u = f(x) and v = g(x) are functions with continuous derivatives, then ∫u dv = uv − ∫v du; the formula, which comes from integrating the product rule, exchanges one integral for another, possibly easier, integral.

concepts.name: Choosing u with LIATE
concepts.statement: To choose u for integration by parts, take the type of function that comes first in the list Logarithmic, Inverse trigonometric, Algebraic, Trigonometric, Exponential; dv is the remaining part of the integrand together with dx, and must be something we can integrate.

concepts.name: Integrating by parts more than once
concepts.statement: When the new integral still cannot be evaluated directly, integration by parts may be applied to it again; if the original integral reappears, it is named I and the equation is solved for I.

concepts.name: Integration by parts for definite integrals
concepts.statement: If u = f(x) and v = g(x) have continuous derivatives on [a, b], then ∫ₐᵇ u dv = uv|ₐᵇ − ∫ₐᵇ v du: the technique is the same, with the step of evaluating at the upper and lower limits of integration added.

concepts.name: Trigonometric integral
concepts.statement: A trigonometric integral is an integral involving powers and products of trigonometric functions.

concepts.name: Power-reducing identities
concepts.statement: sin²x = 1/2 − (1/2)cos(2x) and cos²x = 1/2 + (1/2)cos(2x); they may be derived from the double-angle identity cos(2x) = cos²x − sin²x and the Pythagorean identity cos²x + sin²x = 1, and they turn even powers of sin x and cos x into lower powers.

concepts.name: Integrating powers of sin x and cos x
concepts.statement: To integrate ∫cosʲx sinᵏx dx: if k is odd, keep one sin x, rewrite the rest with sin²x = 1 − cos²x and substitute u = cos x; if j is odd, keep one cos x, rewrite the rest with cos²x = 1 − sin²x and substitute u = sin x; if both are even, use the power-reducing identities, simplify and apply the strategies again.

concepts.name: Products of sines and cosines of different angles
concepts.statement: Products of sin(ax), sin(bx), cos(ax) and cos(bx) are integrated by rewriting each as half a sum or difference of sines or cosines of (a − b)x and (a + b)x; the formulas may be derived from the sum-of-angle formulas for sine and cosine.

concepts.name: Integrating powers of tan x and sec x
concepts.statement: To integrate ∫tanᵏx secʲx dx: if j is even and j ≥ 2, keep sec²x, rewrite the rest with sec²x = tan²x + 1 and substitute u = tan x; if k is odd and j ≥ 1, keep sec x tan x, rewrite the rest with tan²x = sec²x − 1 and substitute u = sec x; if k is odd, k ≥ 3 and j = 0, split off tan²x = sec²x − 1 and repeat; if k is even and j is odd, write tanᵏx in terms of sec x and integrate the odd powers of sec x by parts.

concepts.name: Power reduction formulas
concepts.statement: A power reduction formula allows an integral of a power of a trigonometric function to be exchanged for an integral involving a lower power: ∫secⁿx dx = (1/(n − 1))secⁿ⁻²x tan x + ((n − 2)/(n − 1))∫secⁿ⁻²x dx and ∫tanⁿx dx = (1/(n − 1))tanⁿ⁻¹x − ∫tanⁿ⁻²x dx.

concepts.name: Trigonometric substitution
concepts.statement: Trigonometric substitution is an integration technique that converts an algebraic integral containing expressions of the form √(a² − x²), √(a² + x²) or √(x² − a²) into a trigonometric integral.

concepts.name: Reference triangle
concepts.statement: After a trigonometric substitution, a right triangle drawn from the substitution (for sin θ = x/a, hypotenuse a, the side opposite θ of length x and the third side √(a² − x²)) expresses the trigonometric functions of θ in terms of x, so a result in θ can be written in x; the radical is the length of one side.

concepts.name: Integrating with x = a sin θ
concepts.statement: For an integral involving √(a² − x²), substitute x = a sin θ and dx = a cos θ dθ with −π/2 ≤ θ ≤ π/2, so that √(a² − x²) = a cos θ; evaluate the trigonometric integral and rewrite the result in x with the reference triangle and θ = sin⁻¹(x/a).

concepts.name: Integrating with x = a tan θ
concepts.statement: For an integral involving √(a² + x²), substitute x = a tan θ and dx = a sec²θ dθ with −π/2 < θ < π/2, so that √(a² + x²) = a sec θ; evaluate the trigonometric integral and rewrite the result in x with the reference triangle and θ = tan⁻¹(x/a).

concepts.name: Integrating with x = a sec θ
concepts.statement: For an integral involving √(x² − a²), substitute x = a sec θ and dx = a sec θ tan θ dθ with 0 ≤ θ < π/2 or π/2 < θ ≤ π, so that √(x² − a²) = |a tan θ|, which is a tan θ for x ≥ a and −a tan θ for x ≤ −a; evaluate and rewrite in x with the reference triangle for the sign of x and θ = sec⁻¹(x/a).

concepts.name: Partial fraction decomposition
concepts.statement: Partial fraction decomposition is a technique used to break down a rational function into the sum of simple rational functions; it applies to P(x)/Q(x) only when deg(P(x)) < deg(Q(x)), and otherwise long division first gives A(x) + R(x)/Q(x) with deg(R(x)) < deg(Q(x)).

concepts.name: Nonrepeated linear factors
concepts.statement: If Q(x) factors as (a₁x + b₁)(a₂x + b₂)…(aₙx + bₙ) with each linear factor distinct and deg(P(x)) < deg(Q(x)), there are constants A₁, A₂, …, Aₙ with P(x)/Q(x) = A₁/(a₁x + b₁) + A₂/(a₂x + b₂) + ⋯ + Aₙ/(aₙx + bₙ).

concepts.name: Method of equating coefficients
concepts.statement: After setting the numerators equal, collect each side by powers of x and equate the coefficients of like powers; the system of equations that results is solved for the unknown constants, and it is consistent if and only if the decomposition was set up correctly.

concepts.name: Method of strategic substitution
concepts.statement: Since the equation of numerators must hold for all values of x, substituting carefully chosen values (the zeros of the linear factors) makes all but one term vanish and gives the constants one at a time; the result should be checked by recombining the terms.

concepts.name: Repeated linear factors
concepts.statement: If the denominator contains the repeated linear factor (ax + b)ⁿ, the decomposition must contain A₁/(ax + b) + A₂/(ax + b)² + ⋯ + Aₙ/(ax + b)ⁿ.

concepts.name: Irreducible quadratic
concepts.statement: A quadratic ax² + bx + c is irreducible if ax² + bx + c = 0 has no real zeros, that is, if b² − 4ac < 0.

concepts.name: Irreducible quadratic factors
concepts.statement: For each irreducible quadratic factor ax² + bx + c of Q(x), the decomposition must include (Ax + B)/(ax² + bx + c); for each repeated irreducible quadratic factor (ax² + bx + c)ⁿ, it must include (A₁x + B₁)/(ax² + bx + c) + ⋯ + (Aₙx + Bₙ)/(ax² + bx + c)ⁿ.

concepts.name: Decomposing a rational function
concepts.statement: To decompose P(x)/Q(x): make sure deg(P(x)) < deg(Q(x)), performing long division if not; factor Q(x) into linear and irreducible quadratic factors; let the factors determine the form of the decomposition; solve for the constants; and rewrite the integral in its decomposed form and evaluate it.

concepts.name: Integration table
concepts.statement: An integration table is a table that lists integration formulas; used in the right manner, it is a handy way either to evaluate or to check an integral quickly.

concepts.name: Computer algebra system
concepts.statement: A computer algebra system (CAS) is technology used to perform many mathematical tasks, including integration; it is a faster alternative to a table for solving an integration problem.

concepts.name: Reconciling equivalent antiderivatives
concepts.statement: Two completely correct antiderivatives found by different methods may look very different; they are equivalent as long as they differ by a constant, which identities, algebra or differentiation can show.

concepts.name: Numerical integration
concepts.statement: Numerical integration is the variety of numerical methods used to estimate the value of a definite integral, including the midpoint rule, the trapezoidal rule and Simpson’s rule, when an antiderivative cannot be expressed, or expressed easily, in closed form.

concepts.name: Midpoint rule
concepts.statement: If f(x) is continuous on [a, b], divided into n subintervals of length Δx = (b − a)/n with midpoints mᵢ, then Mₙ = Σ f(mᵢ)Δx, a Riemann sum with subintervals of equal width, satisfies lim Mₙ = ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx as n → ∞.

concepts.name: Trapezoidal rule
concepts.statement: If f(x) is continuous on [a, b], divided into n subintervals of length Δx = (b − a)/n with endpoints x₀, x₁, …, xₙ, then Tₙ = (1/2)Δx(f(x₀) + 2f(x₁) + ⋯ + 2f(xₙ₋₁) + f(xₙ)), the sum of the areas of trapezoids, satisfies lim Tₙ = ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx as n → +∞; Tₙ is the average of the left and right endpoint sums.

concepts.name: Concavity and the trapezoidal and midpoint rules
concepts.statement: For a nonnegative function, the trapezoidal rule tends to overestimate a definite integral over intervals where the function is concave up and to underestimate it where the function is concave down; the midpoint rule partly overestimates and partly underestimates over the same intervals, so it tends to be more accurate.

concepts.name: Absolute error
concepts.statement: If B is an estimate of some quantity having an actual value of A, then the absolute error is |A − B|.

concepts.name: Error bounds for the midpoint and trapezoidal rules
concepts.statement: If f(x) is continuous on [a, b] with a second derivative there and M is the maximum value of |f″(x)| over [a, b], then the error in Mₙ is at most M(b − a)³/(24n²) and the error in Tₙ at most M(b − a)³/(12n²); the bounds tell what n guarantees a given accuracy.

concepts.name: Simpson’s rule
concepts.statement: If f(x) is continuous on [a, b] and n is a positive even integer, with Δx = (b − a)/n and endpoints x₀, …, xₙ, then Sₙ = (Δx/3)(f(x₀) + 4f(x₁) + 2f(x₂) + 4f(x₃) + ⋯ + 2f(xₙ₋₂) + 4f(xₙ₋₁) + f(xₙ)), the integral of a piecewise quadratic function through the points of the graph, satisfies lim Sₙ = ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx as n → +∞; S₂ₙ = (2/3)Mₙ + (1/3)Tₙ.

concepts.name: Error bound for Simpson’s rule
concepts.statement: If f(x) is continuous on [a, b] with a fourth derivative there and M is the maximum value of |f⁽⁴⁾(x)| over [a, b], then the error in Sₙ is at most M(b − a)⁵/(180n⁴).

concepts.name: Improper integral
concepts.statement: An improper integral is an integral over an infinite interval or an integral of a function containing an infinite discontinuity on the interval; it is defined in terms of a limit, and it converges if this limit is a finite real number and diverges otherwise.

concepts.name: Integral over an infinite interval
concepts.statement: For f(x) continuous over [a, +∞), ∫ₐ^{+∞} f(x) dx = lim_{t→+∞} ∫ₐᵗ f(x) dx, provided this limit exists, and likewise over (−∞, b]; over (−∞, +∞) the integral is ∫_{−∞}^0 f(x) dx + ∫₀^{+∞} f(x) dx, provided both converge.

concepts.name: Integral of a discontinuous integrand
concepts.statement: For f(x) continuous over [a, b) and discontinuous at b, ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = lim_{t→b⁻} ∫ₐᵗ f(x) dx, and for f(x) continuous over (a, b], the limit is taken as t → a⁺; if f(x) is continuous over [a, b] except at a point c in (a, b), ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = ∫ₐᶜ f(x) dx + ∫꜀ᵇ f(x) dx, provided both converge.

concepts.name: Gabriel’s Horn
concepts.statement: The solid generated by revolving about the x-axis the region between the graph of f(x) = 1/x and the x-axis over [1, +∞) has a finite volume, π, although the area of the region is infinite.

concepts.name: Comparison theorem for improper integrals
concepts.statement: If f(x) and g(x) are continuous over [a, +∞) with 0 ≤ f(x) ≤ g(x) for x ≥ a, then ∫ₐ^{+∞} f(x) dx = +∞ implies ∫ₐ^{+∞} g(x) dx = +∞, and ∫ₐ^{+∞} g(x) dx = L, a real number, implies ∫ₐ^{+∞} f(x) dx = M for some real number M ≤ L.

concepts.name: Laplace transform
concepts.statement: The Laplace transform of a function f(t) is L{f(t)} = F(s) = ∫₀^∞ e^{−st} f(t) dt, an improper integral that transforms a function of time into a function of frequency; differentiation in the time domain becomes multiplication by s, and integration becomes division by s.

concepts.name: Solution to a differential equation
concepts.statement: A solution to a differential equation is a function y = f(x) that satisfies the differential equation when f and its derivatives are substituted into the equation. A solution is not necessarily unique, since the derivative of a constant is zero.

concepts.name: Order of a differential equation
concepts.statement: The order of a differential equation is the highest order of any derivative of the unknown function that appears in the equation.

concepts.name: General solution
concepts.statement: The general solution, or family of solutions, of a differential equation is the entire set of its solutions; for y′ = 2x it is every function y = x² + C, where C is any constant.

concepts.name: Particular solution
concepts.statement: A particular solution is a member of a family of solutions to a differential equation that satisfies a particular initial condition; additional information, such as a point the solution passes through, can often identify it uniquely.

concepts.name: Initial value
concepts.statement: An initial value is a value or set of values that a solution of a differential equation satisfies for a fixed value of the independent variable, an ordered pair used to find a particular solution. The number of initial values an initial-value problem needs equals the order of the differential equation, all given at the same value of the independent variable.

concepts.name: Solving an initial-value problem
concepts.statement: To solve an initial-value problem, first find the general solution to the differential equation, then substitute the initial value or values to determine the value of the constant, which picks out the particular solution.

concepts.name: Initial velocity
concepts.statement: The initial velocity of an object is its velocity at time t = 0, denoted v(0) = v₀.

concepts.name: Velocity of an object under gravity
concepts.statement: If the only force acting on an object near Earth's surface is gravity, Newton's second law gives m v′(t) = −mg, so v′(t) = −g, whatever the mass, where g ≈ 9.8 m/s²; with the initial velocity v(0) = v₀ the velocity is v(t) = −gt + v₀, and the height s(t) solves the initial-value problem s′(t) = v(t), s(0) = s₀.

concepts.name: Direction field
concepts.statement: A direction field, or slope field, is a mathematical object used to graphically represent solutions to a first-order differential equation y′ = f(x, y): at each point (x, y) a short line segment appears whose slope f(x, y) is equal to the slope of a solution to the differential equation passing through that point.

concepts.name: Solution curve
concepts.statement: A solution curve is a curve graphed in a direction field that corresponds to the solution to the initial-value problem passing through a given point in the field; at each of its points it follows the segment of the field.

concepts.name: Equilibrium solution
concepts.statement: An equilibrium solution of y′ = f(x, y) is any solution of the form y = k, where k is a constant; it is found by setting the right-hand side equal to zero, as any function y = k with f(x, k) = 0 for all x in the domain of f, and in a direction field it shows as horizontal segments all the way across.

concepts.name: Asymptotically stable solution
concepts.statement: An equilibrium solution y = k of y′ = f(x, y) is asymptotically stable if there exists ε > 0 such that for any value c in (k − ε, k + ε) the solution to the initial-value problem y′ = f(x, y), y(x₀) = c approaches k as x approaches infinity.

concepts.name: Asymptotically unstable solution
concepts.statement: An equilibrium solution y = k of y′ = f(x, y) is asymptotically unstable if there exists ε > 0 such that for any value c in (k − ε, k + ε) the solution to the initial-value problem y′ = f(x, y), y(x₀) = c never approaches k as x approaches infinity.

concepts.name: Asymptotically semi-stable solution
concepts.statement: An equilibrium solution y = k is asymptotically semi-stable if it is neither asymptotically stable nor asymptotically unstable: solutions starting on one side of it approach it, and solutions on the other side move away.

concepts.name: Step size
concepts.statement: The step size h is the increment added to the x value at each step in Euler's Method, a small value, typically 0.1 or less; the smaller h, the more calculations and the greater the accuracy.

concepts.name: Euler’s Method
concepts.statement: Euler's Method is a numerical technique that approximates the solution to an initial-value problem y′ = f(x, y), y(x₀) = y₀: from each point it follows the linear approximation with the slope the differential equation gives there for one step h, so xₙ = x₀ + nh and yₙ = yₙ₋₁ + h f(xₙ₋₁, yₙ₋₁).

concepts.name: Separable differential equation
concepts.statement: A separable differential equation is any equation that can be written in the form y′ = f(x)g(y): its right-hand side separates into a function of x times a function of y.

concepts.name: Autonomous differential equation
concepts.statement: An autonomous differential equation is an equation in which the right-hand side is a function of y alone, such as y′ = sec y + tan y.

concepts.name: Separation of variables
concepts.statement: To solve a separable equation y′ = f(x)g(y) by separation of variables: find the values of y that make g(y) = 0, which give constant solutions; rewrite the equation as dy/g(y) = f(x) dx; integrate both sides; solve the resulting equation for y if possible, since often y is found only as an implicit function of x; and, if an initial condition exists, substitute it to find the constant.

concepts.name: Solution concentrations
concepts.statement: The amount u(t) of a substance dissolved in a well-mixed tank changes at the rate it flows in minus the rate it flows out: du/dt = INFLOW RATE − OUTFLOW RATE, where the outflow rate is the concentration u(t)/V of the tank's volume V times the rate the solution drains.

concepts.name: Initial population
concepts.statement: The initial population P₀ is the population at time t = 0.

concepts.name: Growth rate
concepts.statement: The growth rate is the constant r > 0 in the exponential growth function P(t) = P₀e^{rt}, a net (birth minus death) percent growth rate per unit time; in dP/dt = rP the rate at which the population increases is proportional to the population, with r the constant of proportionality.

concepts.name: Carrying capacity
concepts.statement: The carrying capacity K of an organism in a given environment is the maximum population of that organism that the environment can sustain indefinitely; a logistic population approaches it as t approaches infinity.

concepts.name: Logistic differential equation
concepts.statement: The logistic differential equation dP/dt = rP(1 − P/K) is a differential equation that incorporates the carrying capacity K and growth rate r into a population model: while P is small it resembles exponential growth, the growth rate falls as P nears K, the population decreases while P > K, and P = 0 and P = K are its constant solutions.

concepts.name: Phase line
concepts.statement: A phase line is a visual representation of the behavior of solutions to an autonomous differential equation subject to various initial conditions: a line of values of the unknown, marked at the constant solutions, with arrows showing where solutions increase and where they decrease.

concepts.name: Solution of the logistic differential equation
concepts.statement: The solution of the logistic differential equation with initial population P₀, carrying capacity K and growth rate r is P(t) = P₀Ke^{rt}/((K − P₀) + P₀e^{rt}), found by separation of variables and partial fractions; K is a horizontal asymptote of its graph.

concepts.name: Inflection point of the logistic curve
concepts.statement: As long as P₀ < K, the solution of the logistic equation has a point of inflection at t = (1/r) ln((K − P₀)/P₀), where its graph changes from concave up to concave down and the leveling off starts; if P₀ > K the graph has none.

concepts.name: Threshold population
concepts.statement: The threshold population T is the minimum population that is necessary for a species to survive; the threshold population model dP/dt = −rP(1 − P/K)(1 − P/T) incorporates it beside the carrying capacity K.

concepts.name: First-order linear differential equation
concepts.statement: A first-order differential equation is linear if it can be written in the form a(x)y′ + b(x)y = c(x), where a(x), b(x) and c(x) are arbitrary functions of x; terms such as (y′)⁴ or y³ make an equation nonlinear.

concepts.name: Standard form
concepts.statement: The standard form of a first-order linear differential equation is y′ + p(x)y = q(x), obtained by dividing a(x)y′ + b(x)y = c(x) by a(x), so that p(x) = b(x)/a(x) and q(x) = c(x)/a(x).

concepts.name: Integrating factor
concepts.statement: An integrating factor is any function μ(x) that is multiplied on both sides of a differential equation to make the side involving the unknown function equal to the derivative of a product of two functions; for y′ + p(x)y = q(x) it is μ(x) = e^{∫p(x)dx}, which solves the separable equation μ′(x) = μ(x)p(x), so that μ(x)y′ + μ(x)p(x)y = (μ(x)y)′.

concepts.name: Solving a first-order linear differential equation
concepts.statement: To solve a first-order linear differential equation: put it into standard form and identify p(x) and q(x); calculate the integrating factor μ(x) = e^{∫p(x)dx}; multiply both sides of the equation by μ(x); integrate both sides and divide by μ(x), giving y = (1/μ(x))[∫μ(x)q(x)dx + C]; and, if there is an initial condition, determine the value of C.

concepts.name: Free fall with air resistance
concepts.statement: With air resistance proportional to velocity, F_A = −kv for some k > 0, Newton's second law gives the first-order linear initial-value problem m dv/dt = −kv − mg, v(0) = v₀, for the velocity of a rising or falling object.

concepts.name: Kirchhoff’s Loop Rule for a circuit
concepts.statement: Kirchhoff's Loop Rule states that the sum of the voltage drops across the resistors, inductors and capacitors of a closed circuit equals its total electromotive force E: with the drops E_R = Ri, E_L = Li′ and E_C = q/C, Li′ + Ri + q/C = E. With no capacitor it is the first-order linear equation Li′ + Ri = E of an LR circuit; with no inductor, Rq′ + q/C = E of an RC circuit, where i = q′.

concepts.name: Sequence
concepts.statement: An infinite sequence {aₙ} is an ordered list of numbers of the form a₁, a₂, …, aₙ, …. Since a sequence has exactly one value for each positive integer n, it can be described as a function whose domain is the set of positive integers.

concepts.name: Index variable
concepts.statement: The subscript n used to define the terms of a sequence is called the index variable, or index, of the sequence; it need not start at n = 1.

concepts.name: Term of a sequence
concepts.statement: Each number aₙ of the sequence {aₙ} is a term of the sequence, its nth term.

concepts.name: Explicit formula
concepts.statement: A sequence may be defined by an explicit formula aₙ = f(n) for some function f(n) defined over the positive integers.

concepts.name: Recurrence relation
concepts.statement: A recurrence relation is a relationship in which a term aₙ in a sequence is defined in terms of earlier terms in the sequence; one term (or more) is given explicitly, and subsequent terms are defined from the earlier ones.

concepts.name: Graph of a sequence
concepts.statement: The graph of a sequence {aₙ} consists of all points (n, aₙ) for all positive integers n.

concepts.name: Arithmetic sequence
concepts.statement: In an arithmetic sequence the difference between every pair of consecutive terms is the same; in general, an arithmetic sequence is any sequence of the form aₙ = cn + b.

concepts.name: Geometric sequence
concepts.statement: In a geometric sequence the ratio aₙ₊₁/aₙ of every pair of consecutive terms is the same; in general, a geometric sequence is any sequence of the form aₙ = crⁿ.

concepts.name: Limit of a sequence
concepts.statement: Given a sequence {aₙ}, if the terms aₙ become arbitrarily close to a finite number L as n becomes sufficiently large, L is the limit of the sequence, and we write lim_{n→∞} aₙ = L.

concepts.name: Convergent sequence
concepts.statement: A sequence {aₙ} is a convergent sequence if there exists a real number L such that aₙ is arbitrarily close to L as long as n is sufficiently large; it converges to its limit L.

concepts.name: Divergent sequence
concepts.statement: A sequence that is not convergent is divergent, and we say its limit does not exist.

concepts.name: Formal definition of the limit of a sequence
concepts.statement: A sequence {aₙ} converges to a real number L if for all ε > 0 there exists an integer N such that |aₙ − L| < ε if n ≥ N. The convergence or divergence of a sequence depends only on what happens to its terms as n → ∞, so placing finitely many terms before a₁ changes neither it nor the limit.

concepts.name: Divergence to infinity
concepts.statement: A sequence {aₙ} diverges to infinity, written lim_{n→∞} aₙ = ∞, if its terms become arbitrarily large as n → ∞, and to negative infinity if aₙ → −∞; the notation does not mean the limit exists, only why the sequence diverges.

concepts.name: Limit of a sequence defined by a function
concepts.statement: Consider a sequence {aₙ} such that aₙ = f(n) for all n ≥ 1. If there exists a real number L such that lim_{x→∞} f(x) = L, then {aₙ} converges and lim_{n→∞} aₙ = L.

concepts.name: Limit of a geometric sequence
concepts.statement: The geometric sequence {rⁿ} converges to 0 if |r| < 1 and to 1 if r = 1; rⁿ → ∞ if r > 1, and {rⁿ} diverges if r ≤ −1. So {rⁿ} converges if and only if |r| < 1 or r = 1.

concepts.name: Algebraic limit laws for sequences
concepts.statement: Given sequences {aₙ} and {bₙ} and any real number c, if lim aₙ = A and lim bₙ = B, then lim c = c, lim caₙ = cA, lim (aₙ ± bₙ) = A ± B, lim (aₙ · bₙ) = A · B, and lim (aₙ/bₙ) = A/B, provided B ≠ 0 and each bₙ ≠ 0.

concepts.name: Continuous functions defined on convergent sequences
concepts.statement: Consider a sequence {aₙ} that converges to L and a function f continuous at L. Then there exists an integer N such that f is defined at all values aₙ for n ≥ N, and the sequence {f(aₙ)} converges to f(L).

concepts.name: Squeeze Theorem for sequences
concepts.statement: Consider sequences {aₙ}, {bₙ} and {cₙ}, and suppose there exists an integer N such that aₙ ≤ bₙ ≤ cₙ for all n ≥ N. If there exists a real number L such that lim aₙ = L = lim cₙ, then {bₙ} converges and lim bₙ = L.

concepts.name: Bounded above
concepts.statement: A sequence {aₙ} is bounded above if there exists a real number M such that aₙ ≤ M for all positive integers n.

concepts.name: Bounded below
concepts.statement: A sequence {aₙ} is bounded below if there exists a real number M such that M ≤ aₙ for all positive integers n.

concepts.name: Bounded sequence
concepts.statement: A sequence {aₙ} is a bounded sequence if it is bounded above and bounded below, that is, if there exists a constant M such that |aₙ| ≤ M for all positive integers n.

concepts.name: Unbounded sequence
concepts.statement: A sequence that is not bounded is an unbounded sequence.

concepts.name: Convergent sequences are bounded
concepts.statement: If a sequence {aₙ} converges, then it is bounded. Being bounded is a necessary condition for a sequence to converge but not a sufficient one: {(−1)ⁿ} is bounded and diverges.

concepts.name: Monotone sequence
concepts.statement: A sequence {aₙ} is increasing for all n ≥ n₀ if aₙ ≤ aₙ₊₁ for all n ≥ n₀ and decreasing for all n ≥ n₀ if aₙ ≥ aₙ₊₁ for all n ≥ n₀; it is a monotone sequence for all n ≥ n₀ if it is increasing for all n ≥ n₀ or decreasing for all n ≥ n₀. A sequence monotone from some term on is eventually increasing or decreasing.

concepts.name: Monotone Convergence Theorem
concepts.statement: If {aₙ} is a bounded sequence and there exists a positive integer n₀ such that {aₙ} is monotone for all n ≥ n₀, then {aₙ} converges. The condition is sufficient but not necessary.

concepts.name: Fibonacci numbers
concepts.statement: The Fibonacci numbers are defined recursively by F₀ = 0, F₁ = 1 and Fₙ = Fₙ₋₁ + Fₙ₋₂ for n ≥ 2; the ratio Fₙ₊₁/Fₙ of consecutive Fibonacci numbers approaches the golden ratio φ = (1 + √5)/2.

concepts.name: Infinite series
concepts.statement: An infinite series is an expression of the form a₁ + a₂ + a₃ + ⋯ = Σ_{n=1}^∞ aₙ, a sum of infinitely many terms whose value is defined as the limit of its partial sums; its index need not begin at n = 1.

concepts.name: Partial sum
concepts.statement: The kth partial sum of the infinite series Σ aₙ is the finite sum Sₖ = a₁ + a₂ + ⋯ + aₖ; the partial sums form a sequence {Sₖ}.

concepts.name: Convergence of a series
concepts.statement: A series converges if the sequence of its partial sums {Sₖ} converges to a real number S; S is the sum of the series, and we write Σ aₙ = S.

concepts.name: Divergence of a series
concepts.statement: A series diverges if the sequence of its partial sums diverges.

concepts.name: Reindexing a series
concepts.statement: A series whose index begins at a value other than 1 can be reindexed by a change of variables, as m = n − 1 turns Σ_{n=2}^∞ 1/n² into Σ_{m=1}^∞ 1/(m + 1)².

concepts.name: Harmonic series
concepts.statement: The harmonic series is Σ_{n=1}^∞ 1/n = 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/4 + ⋯.

concepts.name: Divergence of the harmonic series
concepts.statement: The harmonic series diverges, though very slowly: its partial sums satisfy S_{2ʲ} > 1 + j/2, so they are unbounded, and after 1,000,000 terms the partial sum is still about 14.4.

concepts.name: Algebraic properties of convergent series
concepts.statement: If Σ aₙ and Σ bₙ are convergent series, then Σ(aₙ + bₙ) converges to Σ aₙ + Σ bₙ (Sum Rule), Σ(aₙ − bₙ) converges to Σ aₙ − Σ bₙ (Difference Rule), and for any real number c, Σ caₙ converges to c Σ aₙ (Constant Multiple Rule).

concepts.name: Geometric series
concepts.statement: A geometric series is a series that can be written in the form a + ar + ar² + ar³ + ⋯ = Σ_{n=1}^∞ arⁿ⁻¹, with initial term a and ratio r.

concepts.name: Sum of a geometric series
concepts.statement: For r ≠ 1 the kth partial sum of a geometric series is Sₖ = a(1 − rᵏ)/(1 − r). If |r| < 1 the series converges and Σ arⁿ⁻¹ = a/(1 − r); if |r| ≥ 1 it diverges.

concepts.name: Writing a repeating decimal as a fraction
concepts.statement: A repeating decimal is a geometric series in disguise: 3.262626… = 3 + 26/10² + 26/10⁴ + ⋯, a geometric series with initial term 26/10² and ratio 1/10² after the 3, whose sum 26/99 gives 3.262626… = 323/99.

concepts.name: Koch snowflake
concepts.statement: Koch’s snowflake is the limit of the figures Fₙ, each made from the last by replacing the middle third of every side with an equilateral triangle pointing outward. Its perimeter 3(4/3)ⁿ grows without bound, while its area, a geometric series, converges to 2√3/5: finite area, infinite perimeter.

concepts.name: Telescoping series
concepts.statement: A telescoping series is a series in which most of the terms cancel in each of the partial sums, leaving only some of the first terms and some of the last terms. For Σ[bₙ − bₙ₊₁], Sₖ = b₁ − bₖ₊₁, so the series converges if and only if {bₖ₊₁} converges, and then its sum is b₁ − lim bₖ₊₁.

concepts.name: Euler’s constant
concepts.statement: The partial sums of the harmonic series behave like the natural logarithm: Σ_{n=1}^{k} 1/n − ln k decreases to a positive limit γ ≈ 0.5772, Euler’s constant.

concepts.name: Divergence test
concepts.statement: If lim_{n→∞} aₙ = c ≠ 0 or the limit does not exist, then the series Σ aₙ diverges. The converse is not true: if aₙ → 0 the test is inconclusive, as the harmonic series shows.

concepts.name: Integral test
concepts.statement: Suppose Σ aₙ is a series with positive terms and there exist a function f and a positive integer N such that f is continuous and decreasing and f(n) = aₙ for all integers n ≥ N. Then Σ aₙ and ∫_N^∞ f(x) dx both converge or both diverge, though their values generally differ.

concepts.name: p-series
concepts.statement: For any real number p, the series Σ_{n=1}^∞ 1/nᵖ is called a p-series; the harmonic series is the p-series with p = 1.

concepts.name: Convergence of p-series
concepts.statement: The p-series Σ 1/nᵖ converges if p > 1 and diverges if p ≤ 1: by the divergence test for p ≤ 0, and by the integral test for p > 0, since ∫_1^∞ 1/xᵖ dx is 1/(p − 1) if p > 1 and ∞ if p ≤ 1.

concepts.name: Remainder of a series
concepts.statement: The remainder R_N = Σ_{n=1}^∞ aₙ − Σ_{n=1}^N aₙ = Σ_{n=N+1}^∞ aₙ is the error made when the sum of a convergent series is approximated by its Nth partial sum.

concepts.name: Remainder estimate from the integral test
concepts.statement: Suppose Σ aₙ is a convergent series with positive terms and f is continuous and decreasing with f(n) = aₙ for all integers n ≥ 1. For all positive integers N, ∫_{N+1}^∞ f(x) dx < R_N < ∫_N^∞ f(x) dx, so S_N + ∫_{N+1}^∞ f(x) dx < Σ aₙ < S_N + ∫_N^∞ f(x) dx.

concepts.name: Comparison test
concepts.statement: Suppose there exists an integer N such that 0 ≤ aₙ ≤ bₙ for all n ≥ N: if Σ bₙ converges, then Σ aₙ converges. Suppose aₙ ≥ bₙ ≥ 0 for all n ≥ N: if Σ bₙ diverges, then Σ aₙ diverges. Geometric series and p-series are the usual series to compare with.

concepts.name: Limit comparison test
concepts.statement: Let aₙ, bₙ ≥ 0 for all n ≥ 1. If lim aₙ/bₙ = L ≠ 0, then Σ aₙ and Σ bₙ both converge or both diverge. If lim aₙ/bₙ = 0 and Σ bₙ converges, then Σ aₙ converges. If lim aₙ/bₙ = ∞ and Σ bₙ diverges, then Σ aₙ diverges. In the other cases the test gives no information.

concepts.name: Alternating series
concepts.statement: Any series whose terms alternate between positive and negative values is an alternating series; it can be written in the form Σ(−1)ⁿ⁺¹bₙ = b₁ − b₂ + b₃ − ⋯ or Σ(−1)ⁿbₙ = −b₁ + b₂ − b₃ + ⋯, where bₙ > 0 for all positive integers n.

concepts.name: Alternating harmonic series
concepts.statement: The alternating harmonic series is Σ(−1)ⁿ⁺¹/n = 1 − 1/2 + 1/3 − 1/4 + ⋯. Whereas the harmonic series diverges, it converges, to ln 2: its odd partial sums decrease and are bounded below, its even ones increase and are bounded above, and both approach one limit.

concepts.name: Alternating series test
concepts.statement: An alternating series Σ(−1)ⁿ⁺¹bₙ or Σ(−1)ⁿbₙ converges if 0 < bₙ₊₁ ≤ bₙ for all n ≥ 1 and lim bₙ = 0; it remains true if 0 < bₙ₊₁ ≤ bₙ only for all n ≥ N.

concepts.name: Remainders in alternating series
concepts.statement: For an alternating series that satisfies the hypotheses of the alternating series test, with sum S and Nth partial sum S_N, the remainder R_N = S − S_N satisfies |R_N| ≤ b_{N+1}: the error is in magnitude at most the size of the next term.

concepts.name: Absolute convergence
concepts.statement: A series Σ aₙ exhibits absolute convergence, or converges absolutely, if Σ |aₙ| converges.

concepts.name: Conditional convergence
concepts.statement: A series Σ aₙ exhibits conditional convergence, or converges conditionally, if Σ aₙ converges but Σ |aₙ| diverges, as the alternating harmonic series does.

concepts.name: Absolute convergence implies convergence
concepts.statement: If Σ |aₙ| converges, then Σ aₙ converges, since 0 ≤ |aₙ| + aₙ ≤ 2|aₙ|.

concepts.name: Riemann Rearrangement Theorem
concepts.statement: Any conditionally convergent series can be rearranged so that the new series diverges or converges to a different real number, as the alternating harmonic series rearranges to 3 ln 2/2; for a series that converges absolutely, every rearrangement has the same sum.

concepts.name: Ratio test
concepts.statement: Let Σ aₙ be a series with nonzero terms and ρ = lim |aₙ₊₁/aₙ|. If 0 ≤ ρ < 1, the series converges absolutely; if ρ > 1 or ρ = ∞, it diverges; if ρ = 1, the test does not provide any information. It suits series whose terms contain factorials or exponentials.

concepts.name: Root test
concepts.statement: Consider the series Σ aₙ and let ρ = lim ⁿ√|aₙ|. If 0 ≤ ρ < 1, the series converges absolutely; if ρ > 1 or ρ = ∞, it diverges; if ρ = 1, the test does not provide any information. It suits series whose terms satisfy |aₙ| = bₙⁿ.

concepts.name: Choosing a convergence test
concepts.statement: To decide whether Σ aₙ converges: ask whether it is a familiar series (harmonic, alternating harmonic, p-series, geometric); whether it is alternating, and whether absolute convergence is wanted; whether it is similar to a p-series or geometric series (comparison or limit comparison test); whether its terms contain a factorial or power (root test for aₙ = bₙⁿ, else ratio test); and last apply the divergence test, then the integral test.

concepts.name: Series converging to π
concepts.statement: Dozens of series converge to π or to an expression in π, at very different rates: the Gregory–Leibniz series π = 4(1 − 1/3 + 1/5 − ⋯), Newton’s series from the arcsine, and Ramanujan’s series for 1/π, which gives many correct digits from its first terms.

concepts.name: Power series
concepts.statement: A series of the form Σₙ₌₀^∞ cₙxⁿ = c₀ + c₁x + c₂x² + ⋯, where x is a variable and the coefficients cₙ are constants, is a power series centered at x = 0; a series of the form Σₙ₌₀^∞ cₙ(x − a)ⁿ is a power series centered at x = a. By convention x⁰ = 1 and (x − a)⁰ = 1 even when x = 0 and x = a.

concepts.name: Convergence of a power series
concepts.statement: A power series Σcₙ(x − a)ⁿ satisfies exactly one of three properties: it converges at x = a and diverges for all x ≠ a; it converges for all real numbers x; or there is a real number R > 0 such that it converges if |x − a| < R and diverges if |x − a| > R, and at the values where |x − a| = R it may converge or diverge.

concepts.name: Interval of convergence
concepts.statement: The interval of convergence of a power series Σcₙ(x − a)ⁿ is the set of real numbers x for which the series converges.

concepts.name: Radius of convergence
concepts.statement: If there is a real number R > 0 such that a power series centered at x = a converges for |x − a| < R and diverges for |x − a| > R, then R is the radius of convergence; if the series converges only at x = a, the radius of convergence is R = 0, and if it converges for all real numbers x, R = ∞.

concepts.name: Finding the interval of convergence
concepts.statement: To find the interval and radius of convergence of a power series, apply the ratio test to the absolute values of its terms: the series converges where the limit ρ < 1 and diverges where ρ > 1; then test each endpoint, where ρ = 1, separately.

concepts.name: Representing functions by geometric series
concepts.statement: Since the geometric series converges to 1/(1 − x) when |x| < 1, the function f(x) = 1/(1 − x) is represented by the power series 1 + x + x² + ⋯ on (−1, 1), and a function of the form g(x)/(1 − h(x)) is represented by substituting into it for the x where |h(x)| < 1.

concepts.name: Combining power series
concepts.statement: If Σcₙxⁿ and Σdₙxⁿ converge to f and g on a common interval I, then Σ(cₙxⁿ ± dₙxⁿ) converges to f ± g on I; for any integer m ≥ 0 and real number b, Σbxᵐcₙxⁿ converges to bxᵐf(x) on I, and Σcₙ(bxᵐ)ⁿ converges to f(bxᵐ) for all x such that bxᵐ is in I.

concepts.name: Multiplying power series
concepts.statement: If Σcₙxⁿ and Σdₙxⁿ converge to f and g on a common interval I and eₙ = c₀dₙ + c₁dₙ₋₁ + ⋯ + cₙd₀ = Σₖ₌₀ⁿ cₖdₙ₋ₖ, then (Σcₙxⁿ)(Σdₙxⁿ) = Σeₙxⁿ, and Σeₙxⁿ, the Cauchy product of the two series, converges to f(x)·g(x) on I.

concepts.name: Term-by-term differentiation and integration
terms: term-by-term differentiation of a power series
term-by-term integration of a power series
concepts.statement: If Σcₙ(x − a)ⁿ converges to f on (a − R, a + R) for some R > 0, then f is differentiable there, f′(x) = Σₙ₌₁^∞ ncₙ(x − a)ⁿ⁻¹, and ∫f(x) dx = C + Σcₙ(x − a)ⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1), both series converging on (a − R, a + R); the behavior at the endpoints must be checked separately.

concepts.name: Uniqueness of power series
concepts.statement: If two convergent power series Σcₙ(x − a)ⁿ and Σdₙ(x − a)ⁿ are equal for all x in an open interval containing a, then cₙ = dₙ for all n ≥ 0.

concepts.name: Present value
concepts.statement: The present value of future payments is their value in terms of today’s dollars, assuming the money can be invested at an interest rate r; payments of C dollars a year for n years are worth C/(1 + r) + C/(1 + r)² + ⋯ + C/(1 + r)ⁿ, and payments that continue indefinitely are worth the sum of a geometric series, C/r.

concepts.name: Taylor series
terms: Taylor series for f at a
concepts.statement: If f has derivatives of all orders at x = a, the Taylor series for f at a is Σₙ₌₀^∞ f⁽ⁿ⁾(a)/n! (x − a)ⁿ = f(a) + f′(a)(x − a) + f″(a)/2! (x − a)² + ⋯; its coefficients are the ones a power series for f at a must have.

concepts.name: Maclaurin series
concepts.statement: The Taylor series for f at 0, Σₙ₌₀^∞ f⁽ⁿ⁾(0)/n! xⁿ, is the Maclaurin series for f.

concepts.name: Uniqueness of Taylor series
concepts.statement: If a function f has a power series at a that converges to f on some open interval containing a, then that power series is the Taylor series for f at a.

concepts.name: Taylor polynomial
concepts.statement: If f has n derivatives at x = a, the nth Taylor polynomial for f at a is pₙ(x) = f(a) + f′(a)(x − a) + f″(a)/2! (x − a)² + ⋯ + f⁽ⁿ⁾(a)/n! (x − a)ⁿ, the nth partial sum of the Taylor series for f at a.

concepts.name: Maclaurin polynomial
concepts.statement: The nth Taylor polynomial for f at 0 is the nth Maclaurin polynomial for f.

concepts.name: Remainder of a Taylor polynomial
concepts.statement: The nth remainder Rₙ(x) = f(x) − pₙ(x) is the error when f(x) is approximated by its nth Taylor polynomial at a; the sequence of Taylor polynomials converges to f exactly where Rₙ converges to zero.

concepts.name: Taylor’s theorem with remainder
concepts.statement: If f can be differentiated n + 1 times on an interval I containing a, then for each x in I there is a real number c between a and x such that Rₙ(x) = f⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾(c)/(n + 1)! (x − a)ⁿ⁺¹; if |f⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾(x)| ≤ M for all x in I, then |Rₙ(x)| ≤ M/(n + 1)! |x − a|ⁿ⁺¹ for all x in I.

concepts.name: Convergence of Taylor series
concepts.statement: If f has derivatives of all orders on an interval I containing a, the Taylor series Σf⁽ⁿ⁾(a)/n! (x − a)ⁿ converges to f(x) for all x in I if and only if lim Rₙ(x) = 0 as n → ∞ for all x in I; the Taylor series for eˣ, sin x and cos x converge to them for all real x.

concepts.name: The irrationality of e
concepts.statement: Supposing e = r/s for integers r and s, the remainder of the nth Maclaurin polynomial of eˣ at 1 makes s n! Rₙ(1) a nonzero integer of magnitude less than 1 for n large, a contradiction, so e is irrational.

concepts.name: Binomial coefficient
concepts.statement: For any real number r, the binomial coefficient is (r choose n) = r(r − 1)(r − 2)⋯(r − n + 1)/n!; for a nonnegative integer r it equals r!/(n!(r − n)!), the coefficient of xⁿ in the binomial expansion of (1 + x)ʳ.

concepts.name: Binomial series
concepts.statement: For any real number r, the Maclaurin series for f(x) = (1 + x)ʳ is the binomial series Σ(r choose n)xⁿ = 1 + rx + r(r − 1)/2! x² + ⋯; it converges to f for |x| < 1, and it terminates when r is a nonnegative integer.

concepts.name: Maclaurin series of common functions
concepts.statement: 1/(1 − x) = Σxⁿ for −1 < x < 1; eˣ = Σxⁿ/n!, sin x = Σ(−1)ⁿx²ⁿ⁺¹/(2n + 1)! and cos x = Σ(−1)ⁿx²ⁿ/(2n)! for all x; ln(1 + x) = Σ(−1)ⁿ⁺¹xⁿ/n for −1 < x ≤ 1; tan⁻¹x = Σ(−1)ⁿx²ⁿ⁺¹/(2n + 1) for −1 ≤ x ≤ 1; (1 + x)ʳ = Σ(r choose n)xⁿ for −1 < x < 1. New Maclaurin series are derived from these by substitution, algebra, differentiation and integration.

concepts.name: Solving a differential equation with power series
concepts.statement: To solve a differential equation by power series, suppose a solution y = Σcₙxⁿ, differentiate it term by term, substitute into the equation, equate the coefficients of like powers of x by the uniqueness of power series, and use the initial conditions to find c₀, c₁ and the rest.

concepts.name: Airy’s equation
concepts.statement: The differential equation y″ − xy = 0 is Airy’s equation; it has no solution in elementary functions, and its power series solutions have coefficients with n(n − 1)cₙ = cₙ₋₃ for n ≥ 3 and c₂ = 0.

concepts.name: Elementary function
concepts.statement: An elementary function is a function that can be written using a finite number of algebraic combinations or compositions of exponential, logarithmic, trigonometric, or power functions.

concepts.name: Nonelementary integral
concepts.statement: An integral ∫f(x) dx whose integrand has no antiderivative that can be written as an elementary function is a nonelementary integral; it can be evaluated by expressing the integrand as a power series and integrating term by term.

concepts.name: Normal distribution
concepts.statement: Data values are normally distributed with mean μ and standard deviation σ when the probability that a randomly chosen value lies between a and b is (1/(σ√(2π)))∫ₐᵇ e^(−(x − μ)²/(2σ²)) dx, the area under a bell-shaped curve; with the z score z = (x − μ)/σ it becomes (1/√(2π))∫ e^(−z²/2) dz from (a − μ)/σ to (b − μ)/σ.

concepts.name: Elliptic integral
concepts.statement: An integral of the form ∫₀^(π/2) dθ/√(1 − k² sin²θ) is an elliptic integral of the first kind; elliptic integrals arose in calculating the arc length of an ellipse and are nonelementary.

concepts.name: Period of a pendulum
concepts.statement: A pendulum of length L making a maximum angle θmax with the vertical has period T = 4√(L/g)∫₀^(π/2) dθ/√(1 − k² sin²θ) with k = sin(θmax/2); expanding the integrand in the binomial series gives T ≈ 2π√(L/g) for small k and T ≈ 2π√(L/g)(1 + k²/4) with two terms.

concepts.name: Parametric equations
concepts.statement: If x and y are continuous functions of t on an interval I, then the equations x = x(t) and y = y(t) are called parametric equations, the equations that define a parametric curve.

concepts.name: Parameter
concepts.statement: The parameter is an independent variable that both x and y depend on in a parametric curve, usually represented by the variable t; it might represent time, or some other meaningful quantity.

concepts.name: Parametric curve
concepts.statement: The set of points (x, y) obtained as t varies over the interval I is called the graph of the parametric equations; the graph is called a parametric curve or plane curve, and is denoted by C.

concepts.name: Orientation
concepts.statement: The orientation of a parametric curve is the direction that a point moves on the graph as the parameter increases.

concepts.name: Eliminating the parameter
concepts.statement: To eliminate the parameter, rewrite the two parametric equations as a single equation relating x and y: solve one equation for t and substitute it into the other, or, where sine and cosine are not one-to-one, combine the equations through an identity such as cos²t + sin²t = 1; the restriction on t restricts the graph.

concepts.name: Parameterization of a curve
concepts.statement: To parameterize the graph of y = f(x), choose x(t), such as x(t) = t or any x(t) whose range is the set of x the graph covers, and substitute it for x in the equation to obtain y(t); a curve can be parameterized in many different ways.

concepts.name: Cycloid
concepts.statement: A cycloid is the curve traced by a point on the rim of a circular wheel as the wheel rolls along a straight line without slippage; a cycloid generated by a wheel of radius a is given by x(t) = a(t − sin t), y(t) = a(1 − cos t).

concepts.name: Hypocycloid
concepts.statement: A hypocycloid is the curve traced by a point on the edge of a circle of radius b rolling around the inside of a larger circle of radius a; the ratio a/b is related to its number of cusps.

concepts.name: Cusp
concepts.statement: A cusp is a pointed end or part where two curves meet, a corner or pointed end of a graph.

concepts.name: Space-filling curve
concepts.statement: A space-filling curve is a curve that completely occupies a two-dimensional subset of the real plane; hypocycloids with an irrational ratio a/b have an infinite number of cusps and never return to their starting point.

concepts.name: Witch of Agnesi
concepts.statement: The witch of Agnesi of a circle of radius a through (0, 0) and (0, 2a) is the path of the point P where the vertical line through B, the point at which the line OA meets the horizontal line through (0, 2a), meets the horizontal line through A, as A moves around the circle; it is parameterized by x = 2a cot θ, y = 2a sin²θ.

concepts.name: Curtate cycloid
concepts.statement: A curtate cycloid is the path of a point on a spoke of a rolling wheel, at a distance b from the center of the wheel that is less than its radius; it has less up-and-down motion than a cycloid.

concepts.name: Prolate cycloid
concepts.statement: A prolate cycloid is the path of a point whose distance b from the center of a rolling wheel is greater than the radius of the wheel, as on the flange of a train wheel; it has loops, where the point travels backward.

concepts.name: Derivative of parametric equations
concepts.statement: For the plane curve defined by x = x(t) and y = y(t), if x′(t) and y′(t) exist and x′(t) ≠ 0, then dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt) = y′(t)/x′(t), the slope of the line tangent to the curve, whether or not the curve is the graph of a function y = f(x).

concepts.name: Second derivative of parametric equations
concepts.statement: The second derivative of a parametric curve is the derivative of dy/dx with respect to x: d²y/dx² = ((d/dt)(dy/dx))/(dx/dt).

concepts.name: Area under a parametric curve
concepts.statement: For the non-self-intersecting plane curve x = x(t), y = y(t), a ≤ t ≤ b, with x(t) differentiable, the area under the curve is A = ∫ₐᵇ y(t)x′(t) dt.

concepts.name: Arc length of a parametric curve
concepts.statement: For the plane curve x = x(t), y = y(t), t₁ ≤ t ≤ t₂, with x(t) and y(t) differentiable, the arc length is s = ∫ √((dx/dt)² + (dy/dt)²) dt from t₁ to t₂, the limit of the lengths of the line segments joining points of a partition of the curve.

concepts.name: Surface area generated by a parametric curve
concepts.statement: The surface area of the volume of revolution generated by revolving the curve x = x(t), y = y(t), a ≤ t ≤ b, around the x-axis is S = 2π∫ₐᵇ y(t)√((x′(t))² + (y′(t))²) dt, provided y(t) is not negative on [a, b]; around the y-axis x(t) takes the place of y(t).

concepts.name: Polar coordinate system
concepts.statement: The polar coordinate system locates each point of the plane by an ordered pair (r, θ): r is the directed distance from the origin to the point, and θ the angle the line segment from the origin to the point makes with the positive x-axis, positive counterclockwise; every point has an infinite number of representations in polar coordinates.

concepts.name: Radial coordinate
concepts.statement: The radial coordinate r is the coordinate in the polar coordinate system that measures the distance from a point in the plane to the pole; a negative r moves along the ray opposite the terminal ray of θ.

concepts.name: Angular coordinate
concepts.statement: The angular coordinate θ is the angle formed by a line segment connecting the origin to a point in the polar coordinate system with the positive radial (x) axis, measured counterclockwise.

concepts.name: Converting points between coordinate systems
concepts.statement: A point with Cartesian coordinates (x, y) and polar coordinates (r, θ) satisfies x = r cos θ and y = r sin θ, and r² = x² + y² and tan θ = y/x; θ is chosen in the quadrant of the point.

concepts.name: Pole
concepts.statement: The pole is the central point of the polar coordinate system, equivalent to the origin of a Cartesian system, where r = 0.

concepts.name: Polar axis
concepts.statement: The polar axis is the horizontal axis of the polar coordinate system corresponding to r ≥ 0, the line segment from the pole going to the right, from which θ is measured.

concepts.name: Polar equation
concepts.statement: A polar equation is an equation or function relating the radial coordinate to the angular coordinate in the polar coordinate system; the graph of a function r = f(θ) is a curve in the polar plane.

concepts.name: Plotting a curve in polar coordinates
concepts.statement: To plot r = f(θ), make a table with a column for θ and one for r, list values of θ, calculate the corresponding r, plot each ordered pair (r, θ), connect the points and look for a pattern, such as periodicity.

concepts.name: Polar curve as a parametric curve
concepts.statement: A curve r = f(θ) is parameterized in rectangular coordinates by x = f(θ) cos θ, y = f(θ) sin θ, with θ as the parameter.

concepts.name: Limaçon
concepts.statement: A limaçon is the graph of the equation r = a + b sin θ or r = a + b cos θ; if a = b the graph is a cardioid.

concepts.name: Cardioid
concepts.statement: A cardioid is a plane curve traced by a point on the perimeter of a circle rolling around a fixed circle of the same radius; its equation is r = a(1 ± cos θ) or r = a(1 ± sin θ), a limaçon in which a = b or a = −b.

concepts.name: Rose
concepts.statement: A rose is the graph of the polar equation r = a cos(bθ) or r = a sin(bθ); if the coefficient of θ is even the graph has twice as many petals as the coefficient, if it is odd the number of petals equals the coefficient, and if it is not an integer the curve closes when it is rational and never closes when it is irrational.

concepts.name: Archimedean spiral
concepts.statement: An Archimedean spiral is the curve r = a + kθ, whose distance from the origin is a constant multiple of the angle plus a constant.

concepts.name: Logarithmic spiral
concepts.statement: A logarithmic spiral is the curve r = a·b^θ; r = 1.2(1.25^θ) describes the shell shape of the chambered nautilus.

concepts.name: Symmetry in polar curves and equations
concepts.statement: A curve r = f(θ) is symmetric about the polar axis if (r, −θ) is on the graph whenever (r, θ) is, about the pole if (r, π + θ) is, and about the vertical line θ = π/2 if (r, π − θ) is; equivalently the equation is unchanged on replacing θ by −θ, r by −r or θ by π + θ, and θ by π − θ.

concepts.name: Area of a sector of a circle
concepts.statement: A sector of a circle of radius r with central angle θ, in radians, is the fraction θ/(2π) of the circle, so its area is A = ½θr².

concepts.name: Area of a region bounded by a polar curve
concepts.statement: If f is continuous and nonnegative on α ≤ θ ≤ β with 0 < β − α ≤ 2π, the area of the region bounded by the graph of r = f(θ) between the radial lines θ = α and θ = β is A = ½∫ [f(θ)]² dθ = ½∫ r² dθ from α to β, the limit of the sums of the areas of sectors.

concepts.name: Area between two polar curves
concepts.statement: To find the area between two polar curves, first find the points of intersection, remembering that the curves may meet at the pole for different values of θ, then subtract the area inside the inner curve from the area inside the outer curve between them.

concepts.name: Arc length of a polar curve
concepts.statement: If f has a continuous derivative on α ≤ θ ≤ β, the length of the graph of r = f(θ) from θ = α to θ = β is L = ∫ √([f(θ)]² + [f′(θ)]²) dθ = ∫ √(r² + (dr/dθ)²) dθ.

concepts.name: Nappe
concepts.statement: A nappe is one half of a double cone; a right circular cone, generated by revolving a line through the origin around the y-axis, has two identically shaped nappes.

concepts.name: Conic section
concepts.statement: A conic section is any curve formed by the intersection of a plane with a cone of two nappes: a hyperbola if the plane intersects both nappes, a parabola if it is parallel to the generating line, a circle if it is perpendicular to the axis of revolution, and an ellipse if it intersects one nappe at an angle to the axis other than 90°.

concepts.name: Focus
concepts.statement: A focus (plural: foci) is a point used to construct and define a conic section; a parabola has one focus; an ellipse and a hyperbola have two.

concepts.name: Directrix
concepts.statement: A directrix (plural: directrices) is a line used to construct and define a conic section; a parabola has one directrix; ellipses and hyperbolas have two.

concepts.name: Vertex of a conic section
concepts.statement: A vertex is an extreme point on a conic section; a parabola has one vertex at its turning point, halfway between the focus and the directrix; an ellipse has two vertices, one at each end of the major axis; a hyperbola has two vertices, one at the turning point of each branch.

concepts.name: Parabola
concepts.statement: A parabola is the set of all points whose distance from a fixed point, called the focus, is equal to the distance from a fixed line, called the directrix; the point halfway between the focus and the directrix is its vertex.

concepts.name: Equation of a parabola in standard form
concepts.statement: A parabola opening upward with vertex (h, k) and focus (h, k + p) has the equation y = (1/(4p))(x − h)² + k, its standard form; its directrix is y = k − p, and the parabolas opening down, right and left have the analogous standard forms.

concepts.name: General form of a conic
concepts.statement: The general form of a conic section is its equation written as a general second-degree equation: ax² + bx + cy + d = 0 or ay² + bx + cy + d = 0 for a parabola, and Ax² + By² + Cx + Dy + E = 0 for an ellipse (A and B of one sign) or a hyperbola (A and B of opposite signs).

concepts.name: Converting a conic to standard form
concepts.statement: To put the general form of a conic into standard form, group the x terms and the y terms, factor out their coefficients, and complete the square in each group, adding the same amount to both sides.

concepts.name: Ellipse
concepts.statement: An ellipse is the set of all points for which the sum of their distances from two fixed points, the foci, is constant, equal to the length 2a of its major axis.

concepts.name: Major axis
concepts.statement: The major axis of a conic section passes through the vertex in the case of a parabola or through the two vertices in the case of an ellipse or hyperbola; it is also an axis of symmetry of the conic; also called the transverse axis.

concepts.name: Minor axis
concepts.statement: The minor axis is perpendicular to the major axis and intersects the major axis at the center of the conic, or at the vertex in the case of the parabola; also called the conjugate axis.

concepts.name: Equation of an ellipse in standard form
concepts.statement: The ellipse with center (h, k), a horizontal major axis of length 2a and a vertical minor axis of length 2b has the equation (x − h)²/a² + (y − k)²/b² = 1, foci (h ± c, k) with c² = a² − b², and directrices x = h ± a²/c; with a vertical major axis, a and b exchange places under (x − h)² and (y − k)².

concepts.name: Hyperbola
concepts.statement: A hyperbola is the set of all points where the difference between their distances from two fixed points, the foci, is constant, equal to 2a; it has two branches, two directrices and two asymptotes.

concepts.name: Equation of a hyperbola in standard form
concepts.statement: The hyperbola with center (h, k) and a horizontal major axis has the equation (x − h)²/a² − (y − k)²/b² = 1, foci (h ± c, k) with c² = a² + b², asymptotes y = k ± (b/a)(x − h) and directrices x = h ± a²/c; with a vertical major axis it is (y − k)²/a² − (x − h)²/b² = 1.

concepts.name: Reflective properties of the conic sections
concepts.statement: Waves coming into a parabolic dish parallel to its axis of symmetry reflect to the focus, and a source at the focus is reflected straight ahead; a ray from one focus of an ellipse passes through the other focus after reflection; a ray directed toward one focus of a hyperbola is reflected by a hyperbolic mirror toward the other focus.

concepts.name: Eccentricity
concepts.statement: The eccentricity e of a conic section is the distance from any point on it to its focus divided by the perpendicular distance from that point to the nearest directrix; it is constant on the conic: e = 1 for a parabola, e < 1 for an ellipse and e > 1 for a hyperbola, with e = c/a for an ellipse or hyperbola, and the eccentricity of a circle is zero.

concepts.name: Focal parameter
concepts.statement: The focal parameter p of a conic section is the distance from a focus to the nearest directrix: a(1 − e²)/e for an ellipse, 2a for a parabola and a(e² − 1)/e for a hyperbola.

concepts.name: Polar equation of a conic section
concepts.statement: With a focus at the pole, a conic section with eccentricity e and focal parameter p has the polar equation r = ep/(1 ± e cos θ), whose major axis is horizontal, or r = ep/(1 ± e sin θ), whose major axis is vertical.

concepts.name: General equation of degree two
concepts.statement: A general equation of degree two has the form Ax² + Bxy + Cy² + Dx + Ey + F = 0; its graph is a conic section, with its axes rotated if B ≠ 0.

concepts.name: Discriminant of a conic section
concepts.statement: The value 4AC − B² of a general equation of degree two, used to identify its conic: an ellipse if 4AC − B² > 0, a parabola if it is 0 and a hyperbola if it is negative.

concepts.name: Rotation of axes
concepts.statement: The axes of a conic Ax² + Bxy + Cy² + Dx + Ey + F = 0 are rotated by the angle θ with cot 2θ = (A − C)/B; in the rotated coordinates the coefficients are A′ = A cos²θ + B cos θ sin θ + C sin²θ, B′ = 0, C′ = A sin²θ − B sin θ cos θ + C cos²θ, D′ = D cos θ + E sin θ, E′ = −D sin θ + E cos θ and F′ = F.

concepts.name: Graphing a rotated conic
concepts.statement: To graph a rotated conic, identify it by the discriminant 4AC − B², determine θ from cot 2θ = (A − C)/B, calculate A′, B′, C′, D′, E′ and F′, rewrite the equation with them, and draw the graph using the rotated equation.

concepts.name: Vector
concepts.statement: A vector is a quantity that has both magnitude and direction; in a plane it is represented by a directed line segment, an arrow, and it is denoted by a boldface letter such as v.

concepts.name: Initial point
concepts.statement: The initial point of a vector is the starting point of the directed line segment that represents it.

concepts.name: Terminal point
concepts.statement: The terminal point of a vector is the endpoint of the directed line segment that represents it; an arrow from the initial point to the terminal point indicates the vector’s direction.

concepts.name: Magnitude of a vector
concepts.statement: The magnitude ‖v‖ of a vector is the length of the line segment that represents it; for v = ⟨x, y⟩ it is ‖v‖ = √(x² + y²), so ‖v‖ ≥ 0, and ‖v‖ = 0 if and only if v = 0.

concepts.name: Zero vector
concepts.statement: The zero vector 0 is the vector whose initial point and terminal point are the same; it is the only vector without a direction, and by convention it can be considered to have any direction convenient to the problem.

concepts.name: Equivalent vectors
concepts.statement: Vectors are equivalent if they have the same magnitude and direction; equivalent vectors are treated as equal, v = w, even if they have different initial points.

concepts.name: Parallel vectors
concepts.statement: Two vectors are parallel if they have the same or opposite directions; two nonzero vectors u and v are parallel if and only if u = kv for some scalar k, and the zero vector is considered parallel to all vectors.

concepts.name: Scalar
concepts.statement: A scalar is a real number; unlike a vector, a scalar has a magnitude only, but no direction.

concepts.name: Scalar multiplication
concepts.statement: The product kv of a vector v and a scalar k is a vector with magnitude |k| times the magnitude of v, with the direction of v if k > 0 and the opposite direction if k < 0; if k = 0 or v = 0, then kv = 0, and (−1)v is written −v. In components, k⟨x₁, y₁⟩ = ⟨kx₁, ky₁⟩.

concepts.name: Vector addition
concepts.statement: The sum v + w is constructed by placing the initial point of w at the terminal point of v; the vector sum is the vector from the initial point of v to the terminal point of w. In components, ⟨x₁, y₁⟩ + ⟨x₂, y₂⟩ = ⟨x₁ + x₂, y₁ + y₂⟩.

concepts.name: Triangle method
concepts.statement: To add two vectors by the triangle method, place the initial point of the second at the terminal point of the first; the sum is the third side of the triangle, from the initial point of the first to the terminal point of the second.

concepts.name: Parallelogram method
concepts.statement: To add two vectors by the parallelogram method, place them with the same initial point and draw the parallelogram with the vectors as two adjacent sides; the sum is the diagonal of the parallelogram from the shared initial point.

concepts.name: Vector difference
concepts.statement: The vector difference v − w is v + (−w) = v + (−1)w; it is drawn from the terminal point of w to the terminal point of v when v and w share an initial point.

concepts.name: Triangle inequality for vectors
concepts.statement: Because v, w and v + w form the sides of a triangle, ‖v + w‖ ≤ ‖v‖ + ‖w‖, with equality only when v and w have the same direction.

concepts.name: Standard-position vector
concepts.statement: A vector with its initial point at the origin is a standard-position vector; it is described by the coordinates of its terminal point.

concepts.name: Component form of a vector
concepts.statement: The vector with initial point (0, 0) and terminal point (x, y) can be written in component form as v = ⟨x, y⟩, with angle brackets for a vector and parentheses for a point; the scalars x and y are the components of v.

concepts.name: Component form of a vector from its points
concepts.statement: If v has initial point (xᵢ, yᵢ) and terminal point (xₜ, yₜ), then v = ⟨xₜ − xᵢ, yₜ − yᵢ⟩: subtract the coordinates of the initial point from those of the terminal point.

concepts.name: Properties of vector operations
concepts.statement: For vectors u, v, w and scalars r, s: u + v = v + u; (u + v) + w = u + (v + w); u + 0 = u; u + (−u) = 0; r(su) = (rs)u; (r + s)u = ru + su; r(u + v) = ru + rv; 1u = u and 0u = 0.

concepts.name: Components from magnitude and direction
concepts.statement: If a vector v forms the angle θ with the positive x-axis, its components are ⟨‖v‖cos θ, ‖v‖sin θ⟩, the legs of a right triangle with the vector as its hypotenuse.

concepts.name: Unit vector
terms: unit vector in the direction of
concepts.statement: A unit vector is a vector with magnitude 1; for any nonzero vector v, u = (1/‖v‖)v is the unit vector in the direction of v.

concepts.name: Normalization
concepts.statement: Normalization is using scalar multiplication to find a unit vector with a given direction: multiply the vector by the reciprocal of its magnitude.

concepts.name: Standard unit vectors
concepts.statement: The standard unit vectors are i = ⟨1, 0⟩ and j = ⟨0, 1⟩, unit vectors along the coordinate axes; any vector can be written as the linear combination v = ⟨x, y⟩ = xi + yj.

concepts.name: Three-dimensional rectangular coordinate system
concepts.statement: The three-dimensional rectangular coordinate system consists of three perpendicular axes, the x-, y- and z-axes, meeting at the origin; every point in space is described by an ordered triple (x, y, z), and the system is denoted ℝ³.

concepts.name: Right-hand rule
concepts.statement: The coordinate axes follow the right-hand rule: when the fingers of the right hand point along the positive x-axis and curl toward the positive y-axis, the thumb points along the positive z-axis.

concepts.name: Coordinate planes
concepts.statement: Each pair of coordinate axes forms a coordinate plane: the xy-plane {(x, y, 0)}, the xz-plane {(x, 0, z)} and the yz-plane {(0, y, z)}.

concepts.name: Octants
concepts.statement: The coordinate planes divide space into eight regions about the origin, called octants; points in an octant have three nonzero coordinates.

concepts.name: Distance between two points in space
concepts.statement: The distance d between points (x₁, y₁, z₁) and (x₂, y₂, z₂) is d = √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)² + (z₂ − z₁)²), the length of the diagonal of the rectangular prism with the two points as opposite corners.

concepts.name: Equations of planes parallel to coordinate planes
concepts.statement: The plane parallel to the xy-plane through (a, b, c) is z = c, the plane parallel to the xz-plane is y = b, and the plane parallel to the yz-plane is x = a.

concepts.name: Sphere
concepts.statement: A sphere is the set of all points in space equidistant from a fixed point, the center of the sphere; the distance from the center to a point on the sphere is the radius.

concepts.name: Standard equation of a sphere
concepts.statement: The sphere with center (a, b, c) and radius r can be represented by the equation (x − a)² + (y − b)² + (z − c)² = r², the standard equation of a sphere.

concepts.name: Vectors in three dimensions
concepts.statement: A three-dimensional vector v = ⟨x, y, z⟩ is the directed line segment from (0, 0, 0) to (x, y, z); with the standard unit vectors i = ⟨1, 0, 0⟩, j = ⟨0, 1, 0⟩ and k = ⟨0, 0, 1⟩, v = xi + yj + zk, and 0 = ⟨0, 0, 0⟩.

concepts.name: Properties of vectors in space
concepts.statement: For v = ⟨x₁, y₁, z₁⟩, w = ⟨x₂, y₂, z₂⟩ and a scalar k: kv = ⟨kx₁, ky₁, kz₁⟩; v + w = ⟨x₁ + x₂, y₁ + y₂, z₁ + z₂⟩; v − w = ⟨x₁ − x₂, y₁ − y₂, z₁ − z₂⟩; ‖v‖ = √(x₁² + y₁² + z₁²); and v/‖v‖ is the unit vector in the direction of v ≠ 0.

concepts.name: Graphing equations in three dimensions
