concepts.statement: The same equation can describe a point, a line or a plane in ℝ, ℝ² and ℝ³; to graph an equation in space, find which coordinates it restricts (a product equal to zero gives the union of the sets where each factor is zero, and an equation free of one variable extends its graph in that variable’s direction).

concepts.name: Dot product
concepts.statement: The dot product of u = ⟨u₁, u₂, u₃⟩ and v = ⟨v₁, v₂, v₃⟩ is the scalar u·v = u₁v₁ + u₂v₂ + u₃v₃, the sum of the products of the components; it is also called the scalar product or inner product.

concepts.name: Properties of the dot product
concepts.statement: For vectors u, v, w and a scalar c: u·v = v·u; u·(v + w) = u·v + u·w; c(u·v) = (cu)·v = u·(cv); and v·v = ‖v‖².

concepts.name: Angle between two vectors
concepts.statement: Two nonzero vectors placed in standard position form an angle θ between them, the smallest one, with 0 ≤ θ ≤ π.

concepts.name: Dot product and the angle between vectors
concepts.statement: The dot product of two vectors is the product of their magnitudes and the cosine of the angle between them, u·v = ‖u‖‖v‖cos θ, so cos θ = u·v/(‖u‖‖v‖) gives the angle between nonzero vectors.

concepts.name: Orthogonal vectors
concepts.statement: The nonzero vectors u and v are orthogonal, forming a right angle when placed in standard position, if and only if u·v = 0; vectors are orthogonal, lines perpendicular, and normal is used of a plane or surface.

concepts.name: Direction angles
concepts.statement: The angles a nonzero vector forms with the coordinate axes, α with i, β with j and γ with k, are its direction angles.

concepts.name: Direction cosines
concepts.statement: The cosines of a vector’s direction angles are its direction cosines; for v, cos α = v·i/‖v‖, and likewise with j and k.

concepts.name: Vector projection
concepts.statement: The vector projection of v onto u is the component of v that acts in the direction of u, proj_u v = (u·v/‖u‖²)u; it has the initial point of u and v, the direction of u, and the opposite direction when the angle between them is obtuse.

concepts.name: Scalar projection
concepts.statement: The scalar projection of v onto u, the length of the vector projection, is comp_u v = u·v/‖u‖.

concepts.name: Resolving a vector into orthogonal components
terms: resolution of a vector into components
concepts.statement: To decompose v into orthogonal components with one in the direction of u, take p = proj_u v and q = v − p; then v = p + q and p·q = 0.

concepts.name: Work done by a constant force
concepts.statement: When a constant force F moves an object in a straight line from P to Q, acting at an angle θ from the line of motion, the work done is W = F·PQ⃗ = ‖F‖‖PQ⃗‖cos θ, the dot product of the force and the displacement.

concepts.name: Cross product
concepts.statement: The cross product of u = ⟨u₁, u₂, u₃⟩ and v = ⟨v₁, v₂, v₃⟩ is the vector u × v = (u₂v₃ − u₃v₂)i − (u₁v₃ − u₃v₁)j + (u₁v₂ − u₂v₁)k, orthogonal to both u and v; it is also called the vector product.

concepts.name: Direction of the cross product
concepts.statement: The direction of u × v is given by the right-hand rule: with the fingers of the right hand along u, curled toward v, the thumb points along u × v; so v × u points the opposite way.

concepts.name: Cross products of the standard unit vectors
concepts.statement: i × i = j × j = k × k = 0; i × j = k, j × k = i, k × i = j; and j × i = −k, k × j = −i, i × k = −j.

concepts.name: Properties of the cross product
concepts.statement: For vectors u, v, w and a scalar c: u × v = −(v × u) (anticommutative); u × (v + w) = u × v + u × w; c(u × v) = (cu) × v = u × (cv); u × 0 = 0 × u = 0; v × v = 0; and u·(v × w) = (u × v)·w.

concepts.name: Magnitude of the cross product
concepts.statement: If θ is the angle between u and v, then ‖u × v‖ = ‖u‖‖v‖sin θ.

concepts.name: Determinant
terms: expansion of the determinant along the first row
concepts.statement: A determinant is a real number associated with a square matrix: a 2 × 2 determinant is a₁b₂ − b₁a₂, and a 3 × 3 determinant is defined by expansion along the first row, each entry of the first row times the 2 × 2 determinant left when its row and column are crossed out, with the middle term subtracted.

concepts.name: Cross product calculated by a determinant
concepts.statement: The cross product u × v is the determinant with i, j, k in the first row, the components of u in the second and those of v in the third, expanded along the first row.

concepts.name: Area of a parallelogram
concepts.statement: If vectors u and v form adjacent sides of a parallelogram, its area is ‖u × v‖, its base ‖u‖ times its height ‖v‖sin θ; a triangle with those sides has half that area.

concepts.name: Triple scalar product
concepts.statement: The triple scalar product of u, v and w is u·(v × w), the dot product of a vector with the cross product of two others; it is the determinant of the 3 × 3 matrix whose rows are the components of u, v and w, and it changes sign when two of the vectors trade places.

concepts.name: Parallelepiped
concepts.statement: A parallelepiped is a three-dimensional prism with six faces that are each parallelograms; three vectors with one initial point, not in one plane, form three of its edges.

concepts.name: Volume of a parallelepiped
concepts.statement: The volume of a parallelepiped with adjacent edges u, v and w is the absolute value of the triple scalar product, V = |u·(v × w)|, the area ‖v × w‖ of its base times its height ‖proj_{v×w} u‖; the triple scalar product is zero exactly when the vectors are coplanar.

concepts.name: Torque
concepts.statement: Torque τ measures the tendency of a force to produce rotation about an axis: if r runs from a point on the axis of rotation to the point where the force F is applied, τ = r × F, and ‖τ‖ = ‖r‖‖F‖sin θ.

concepts.name: Direction vector
concepts.statement: A direction vector of a line in space is a vector parallel to the line, used to describe its direction.

concepts.name: Vector equation of a line
concepts.statement: A line through P(x₀, y₀, z₀) with direction vector v = ⟨a, b, c⟩ is described by r = r₀ + tv, where r = ⟨x, y, z⟩ and r₀ = ⟨x₀, y₀, z₀⟩ is the position vector of P, since PQ⃗ = tv for every point Q on the line.

concepts.name: Parametric equations of a line
concepts.statement: A line L parallel to v = ⟨a, b, c⟩ through P(x₀, y₀, z₀) is described by the parametric equations x = x₀ + ta, y = y₀ + tb, z = z₀ + tc; they are not unique.

concepts.name: Symmetric equations of a line
concepts.statement: If a, b and c are all nonzero, the line parallel to ⟨a, b, c⟩ through (x₀, y₀, z₀) is described by the symmetric equations (x − x₀)/a = (y − y₀)/b = (z − z₀)/c.

concepts.name: Equation of a line segment
concepts.statement: The line segment from P to Q, with position vectors p and q, is r = (1 − t)p + tq for 0 ≤ t ≤ 1; in components x = x₀ + t(x₁ − x₀), y = y₀ + t(y₁ − y₀), z = z₀ + t(z₁ − z₀), 0 ≤ t ≤ 1.

concepts.name: Distance from a point to a line
concepts.statement: If a line L passes through P with direction vector v and M is a point not on L, the distance from M to L, the length of the perpendicular segment, is d = ‖PM⃗ × v‖/‖v‖, the height of the parallelogram on PM⃗ and v.

concepts.name: Skew lines
concepts.statement: Two lines in space that are not parallel and do not intersect are skew lines.

concepts.name: Classifying lines in space
concepts.statement: Two lines in space are equal, parallel but not equal, intersecting or skew, decided by whether their direction vectors are parallel and whether they share a point (solving their parametric equations together).

concepts.name: Normal vector
concepts.statement: A normal vector n of a plane is a vector perpendicular to it: every vector PQ⃗ between points of the plane is orthogonal to n.

concepts.name: Vector equation of a plane
concepts.statement: Given a point P and a vector n, the set of all points Q satisfying n·PQ⃗ = 0 forms a plane; n·PQ⃗ = 0 is the vector equation of the plane.

concepts.name: Scalar equation of a plane
terms: general form of the equation of a plane
concepts.statement: The scalar equation of the plane through P = (x₀, y₀, z₀) with normal vector n = ⟨a, b, c⟩ is a(x − x₀) + b(y − y₀) + c(z − z₀) = 0, which can be written in the general form ax + by + cz + d = 0 with d = −ax₀ − by₀ − cz₀.

concepts.name: Distance from a point to a plane
concepts.statement: If a plane with normal vector n passes through Q, the distance from the plane to a point P not in it is d = ‖proj_n QP⃗‖ = |comp_n QP⃗| = |QP⃗·n|/‖n‖; for the plane ax + by + cz + k = 0 and P(x₀, y₀, z₀), d = |ax₀ + by₀ + cz₀ + k|/√(a² + b² + c²).

concepts.name: Parallel and intersecting planes
concepts.statement: Two distinct planes are parallel, when their normal vectors are parallel, or they intersect, and the intersection of two nonparallel planes is always a line; the distance between parallel planes is the distance from a point of one to the other.

concepts.name: Angle between two planes
concepts.statement: The angle θ between two intersecting planes has the measure of the angle between their normal vectors, cos θ = |n₁·n₂|/(‖n₁‖‖n₂‖).

concepts.name: Surface
concepts.statement: Planes, spheres and cylinders are examples of three-dimensional figures called surfaces, which can be graphed in a three-dimensional coordinate system.

concepts.name: Cylindrical surface
concepts.statement: A set of lines parallel to a given line passing through a given curve is a cylindrical surface, or cylinder; any curve in one of the coordinate planes extends to a cylinder, such as x² + y² = 9 in space.

concepts.name: Rulings
concepts.statement: The parallel lines that make up a cylinder are its rulings.

concepts.name: Trace
concepts.statement: The traces of a surface are the cross-sections created when it intersects a plane parallel to one of the coordinate planes; to find the trace in the xy-, yz- or xz-plane, set z = 0, x = 0 or y = 0.

concepts.name: Quadric surface
concepts.statement: Quadric surfaces are the graphs of equations Ax² + By² + Cz² + Dxy + Exz + Fyz + Gx + Hy + Jz + K = 0; when a quadric surface intersects a coordinate plane, the trace is a conic section.

concepts.name: Ellipsoid
concepts.statement: An ellipsoid is a surface x²/a² + y²/b² + z²/c² = 1, all of whose traces are ellipses; a sphere is an ellipsoid with a = b = c.

concepts.name: Elliptic paraboloid
concepts.statement: An elliptic paraboloid is a surface x²/a² + y²/b² = z/c, whose traces include ellipses and parabolas; interchanging the variables gives other orientations.

concepts.name: Hyperboloid of one sheet
concepts.statement: A hyperboloid of one sheet is a surface x²/a² + y²/b² − z²/c² = 1, whose traces include ellipses and hyperbolas; it can be constructed of straight lines.

concepts.name: Hyperboloid of two sheets
concepts.statement: A hyperboloid of two sheets is a surface z²/c² − x²/a² − y²/b² = 1, whose traces include ellipses and hyperbolas.

concepts.name: Elliptic cone
concepts.statement: An elliptic cone is a surface x²/a² + y²/b² − z²/c² = 0, whose traces include ellipses and intersecting lines.

concepts.name: Hyperbolic paraboloid
concepts.statement: A hyperbolic paraboloid is a saddle-shaped surface z/c = x²/a² − y²/b², whose traces include hyperbolas and parabolas.

concepts.name: Sketching a surface from its traces
concepts.statement: To sketch a quadric surface, sketch its traces in the coordinate planes (and in parallel planes where a trace is a single point), which give the framework of the surface.

concepts.name: Identifying quadric surfaces
concepts.statement: To identify the surface of a second-degree equation, look at the signs and powers of x, y and z, completing the square where a variable appears to the first power as well, and match the standard form.

concepts.name: Cylindrical coordinate system
concepts.statement: In the cylindrical coordinate system a point in space is represented by the ordered triple (r, θ, z), where (r, θ) are the polar coordinates of its projection in the xy-plane and z is the usual z-coordinate.

concepts.name: Conversion between cylindrical and rectangular coordinates
concepts.statement: Rectangular and cylindrical coordinates of a point are related by x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ, z = z, and r² = x² + y², tan θ = y/x, z = z, θ chosen by the quadrant of (x, y).

concepts.name: Spherical coordinate system
concepts.statement: In the spherical coordinate system a point P in space is represented by (ρ, θ, φ), where ρ is the distance between P and the origin (ρ ≠ 0), θ is the angle of cylindrical coordinates, and φ is the angle between the positive z-axis and the segment OP, 0 ≤ φ ≤ π.

concepts.name: Conversion among spherical, cylindrical and rectangular coordinates
concepts.statement: Spherical and rectangular coordinates are related by x = ρ sin φ cos θ, y = ρ sin φ sin θ, z = ρ cos φ, and ρ² = x² + y² + z², tan θ = y/x, φ = arccos(z/√(x² + y² + z²)); spherical and cylindrical by r = ρ sin φ, θ = θ, z = ρ cos φ, and ρ = √(r² + z²), φ = arccos(z/√(r² + z²)).

concepts.name: Surfaces of constant coordinate
concepts.statement: Holding one coordinate constant gives a surface: in rectangular coordinates x = c, y = c, z = c are planes; in cylindrical coordinates r = c is a vertical circular cylinder, θ = c a half-plane from the z-axis, z = c a plane; in spherical coordinates ρ = c is a sphere, θ = c a half-plane and φ = c a half-cone.

concepts.name: Latitude and longitude
concepts.statement: Latitude and longitude locate points on Earth’s surface as spherical coordinates: with the z-axis through the North Pole and the prime meridian in the xz-plane, longitude east is θ, west negative, and φ is 90° minus the latitude north.

concepts.name: Choosing a coordinate system
concepts.statement: Choose the coordinate system by the problem’s symmetry: spherical coordinates for symmetry about a point, cylindrical coordinates for symmetry about an axis, rectangular coordinates where there is neither, and orient the axes to suit the problem.

concepts.name: Vector-valued function
concepts.statement: A vector-valued function is a function of the form r(t) = f(t) i + g(t) j or r(t) = f(t) i + g(t) j + h(t) k, also written r(t) = ⟨f(t), g(t)⟩ or ⟨f(t), g(t), h(t)⟩, where the component functions f, g and h are real-valued functions of the parameter t. Its domain consists of real numbers and its range of two- or three-dimensional vectors.

concepts.name: Component functions
concepts.statement: The component functions of the vector-valued function r(t) = f(t) i + g(t) j are f(t) and g(t), and the component functions of r(t) = f(t) i + g(t) j + h(t) k are f(t), g(t) and h(t); they are real-valued functions of the parameter t.

concepts.name: Space curve
concepts.statement: The graph of a vector-valued function r(t) = f(t) i + g(t) j + h(t) k, its vectors graphed in standard position, traces a space curve: the set of ordered triples (f(t), g(t), h(t)) together with their defining parametric equations x = f(t), y = g(t) and z = h(t).

concepts.name: Vector parameterization
concepts.statement: Any representation of a plane curve or space curve using a vector-valued function is called a vector parameterization of the curve; an arbitrary plane curve can be represented by one.

concepts.name: Helix
concepts.statement: A helix is a three-dimensional curve in the shape of a spiral; r(t) = 4 cos t i + 4 sin t j + t k resembles a spring with a circular cross-section looking down along the z-axis, and a helix may also be elliptical in cross-section. A helix of radius R and height h that completes N turns is r(t) = R cos(2πNt/h) i + R sin(2πNt/h) j + t k, 0 ≤ t ≤ h.

concepts.name: Reparameterization
concepts.statement: A reparameterization is an alternative parameterization of a given vector-valued function: replacing t with 2t, say, traces the same curve while the interval over which t is defined may change. Any curve has an infinite number of reparameterizations.

concepts.name: Limit of a vector-valued function
concepts.statement: A vector-valued function r approaches the limit L as t approaches a, written lim_{t→a} r(t) = L, provided lim_{t→a} ‖r(t) − L‖ = 0.

concepts.name: Limit of a vector-valued function by components
concepts.statement: Let f, g and h be functions of t. The limit of r(t) = f(t) i + g(t) j + h(t) k as t approaches a is [lim f(t)] i + [lim g(t)] j + [lim h(t)] k, provided the limits of the component functions exist; to calculate the limit of a vector-valued function, calculate the limits of the component functions separately.

concepts.name: Continuity of a vector-valued function
concepts.statement: A vector-valued function r(t) is continuous at the point t = a if r(a) exists, lim_{t→a} r(t) exists, and lim_{t→a} r(t) = r(a).

concepts.name: Derivative of a vector-valued function
concepts.statement: The derivative of a vector-valued function r(t) is r′(t) = lim_{Δt→0} [r(t + Δt) − r(t)]/Δt, provided the limit exists; then r is differentiable at t. Its range consists of vectors, and when r represents the position of an object, r′ represents its velocity.

concepts.name: Differentiation of vector-valued functions
concepts.statement: Let f, g and h be differentiable functions of t. If r(t) = f(t) i + g(t) j, then r′(t) = f′(t) i + g′(t) j; if r(t) = f(t) i + g(t) j + h(t) k, then r′(t) = f′(t) i + g′(t) j + h′(t) k. To calculate the derivative, differentiate the component functions.

concepts.name: Properties of the derivative of vector-valued functions
concepts.statement: Let r and u be differentiable vector-valued functions of t, f a differentiable real-valued function of t and c a scalar. Then d/dt[c r] = c r′, d/dt[r ± u] = r′ ± u′, d/dt[f u] = f′ u + f u′, d/dt[r · u] = r′ · u + r · u′, d/dt[r × u] = r′ × u + r × u′ and d/dt[r(f(t))] = r′(f(t)) · f′(t).

concepts.name: A vector-valued function of constant magnitude
concepts.statement: If r(t) · r(t) = c, a constant, then r(t) · r′(t) = 0: a vector-valued function of constant magnitude is orthogonal to its derivative. It follows from the dot product rule, since 2 r(t) · r′(t) = d/dt[c] = 0.

concepts.name: Tangent vector
concepts.statement: Let C be a curve defined by a vector-valued function r, and assume that r′(t₀) exists. A tangent vector v at t = t₀ is any vector such that, when the tail of the vector is placed at the point r(t₀) on the graph, v is tangent to the curve C; r′(t₀) is one.

concepts.name: Principal unit tangent vector
concepts.statement: Assume r′(t) ≠ 0. The principal unit tangent vector at t is T(t) = r′(t)/‖r′(t)‖, a unit vector tangent to the curve C.

concepts.name: Finding a unit tangent vector
concepts.statement: To calculate a unit tangent vector, first find the derivative r′(t), second calculate its magnitude ‖r′(t)‖, and third divide the derivative by its magnitude.

concepts.name: Indefinite integral of a vector-valued function
terms: indefinite integral of a vector-valued function
concepts.statement: The indefinite integral of a vector-valued function r(t) = f(t) i + g(t) j + h(t) k is [∫ f(t) dt] i + [∫ g(t) dt] j + [∫ h(t) dt] k, a vector-valued function whose derivative is r(t); each component integral contains its own constant, so the integration constant becomes a constant vector C.

concepts.name: Definite integral of a vector-valued function
terms: definite integral of a vector-valued function
concepts.statement: The definite integral of a vector-valued function over [a, b] is the vector obtained by calculating the definite integral of each of the component functions over [a, b], then using the results as the components of the resulting vector.

concepts.name: Smooth curve
concepts.statement: A smooth curve is one whose vector-valued function r(t) is continuously differentiable with a nonzero derivative; smoothness guarantees that the curve has no cusps or corners.

concepts.name: Arc length of a curve given by a vector-valued function
concepts.statement: Given a smooth curve C defined by r(t) = f(t) i + g(t) j + h(t) k for t in [a, b], the arc length of C over the interval is s = ∫ₐᵇ √([f′(t)]² + [g′(t)]² + [h′(t)]²) dt = ∫ₐᵇ ‖r′(t)‖ dt; a plane curve has two component functions under the root instead of three.

concepts.name: Arc length of a helix
concepts.statement: The length of a wire needed to form a helix with N turns that has radius R and height h is s = √(4π²N²R² + h²), since ‖r′(t)‖ is constant along the helix.

concepts.name: Arc-length function
concepts.statement: Let r(t) describe a smooth curve for t ≥ a. The arc-length function s(t) = ∫ₐᵗ ‖r′(u)‖ du measures the arc length of the curve as a function of t, how far a particle travels; ds/dt = ‖r′(t)‖ > 0, and if ‖r′(t)‖ = 1 for all t ≥ a, the parameter t represents the arc length from the starting point at t = a.

concepts.name: Arc-length parameterization
concepts.statement: An arc-length parameterization is a reparameterization of a vector-valued function in which the parameter is equal to the arc length: solving the arc-length function s(t) for t and substituting into r(t) writes the curve as r(s), and the distance traveled along the curve starting from s = 0 equals s.

concepts.name: Finding an arc-length parameterization
concepts.statement: Find the arc-length function s(t) = ∫ₐᵗ ‖r′(u)‖ du, solve it for t as a function of s, and replace t in r(t) with that expression; the restriction on t becomes a restriction on s.

concepts.name: Curvature
concepts.statement: Let C be a smooth curve in the plane or in space given by r(s), where s is the arc-length parameter. The curvature κ at s is κ = ‖dT/ds‖ = ‖T′(s)‖, the derivative of the unit tangent vector with respect to arc length. It measures how sharply the curve turns: the curvature of a circle is constant and equal to the reciprocal of its radius, and the curvature of a curve at a point is that of the circle that hugs it there.

concepts.name: Alternative formulas for curvature
concepts.statement: If C is a smooth curve given by r(t), its curvature at t is κ = ‖T′(t)‖/‖r′(t)‖; if C is three-dimensional, κ = ‖r′(t) × r″(t)‖/‖r′(t)‖³; and if C is the graph of y = f(x) with y′ and y″ existing, κ = |y″|/[1 + (y′)²]^{3/2}.

concepts.name: Principal unit normal vector
concepts.statement: Let C be a three-dimensional smooth curve represented by r over an open interval I. If T′(t) ≠ 0, the principal unit normal vector at t is N(t) = T′(t)/‖T′(t)‖, a unit vector orthogonal to the unit tangent vector, pointing toward the side the curve turns to.

concepts.name: Binormal vector
concepts.statement: The binormal vector at t is B(t) = T(t) × N(t), a unit vector orthogonal to both the unit tangent vector and the unit normal vector.

concepts.name: Normal plane
concepts.statement: The unit normal vector and the binormal vector form a plane that is perpendicular to the curve at any point on the curve, called the normal plane.

concepts.name: Frenet frame of reference
concepts.statement: At every point of a smooth curve in three dimensions the unit tangent vector T, the principal unit normal vector N and the binormal vector B form a frame of reference called the Frenet frame of reference, or the TNB frame.

concepts.name: Osculating plane
concepts.statement: The plane determined by the unit tangent vector T and the unit normal vector N is the osculating plane of C at a point P on the curve.

concepts.name: Radius of curvature
concepts.statement: The radius of curvature of a curve at a point is the reciprocal of the curvature, r = 1/κ, the radius of the circle in the osculating plane that has the curve's curvature at that point.

concepts.name: Osculating circle
concepts.statement: The osculating circle of C at P is the circle in the osculating plane that lies on the concave side of the curve, is tangent to the curve at P and shares the curve's curvature there; its radius is the radius of curvature.

concepts.name: Finding the equation of an osculating circle
concepts.statement: To find an osculating circle of a curve y = f(x) in two dimensions, calculate the curvature at the point, take its reciprocal as the radius, locate the center that distance from the point along the normal on the concave side, and write (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r².

concepts.name: Velocity vector
concepts.statement: Let r(t) be a twice-differentiable vector-valued function of the parameter t that represents the position of an object as a function of time. The velocity vector of the object is v(t) = r′(t), the derivative of the position vector; it is always tangent to the path.

concepts.name: Acceleration vector
concepts.statement: The acceleration vector of an object with position r(t) is a(t) = v′(t) = r″(t), the second derivative of the position vector; it always points toward the concave side of the path.

concepts.name: Speed along a path
concepts.statement: The speed of an object with position r(t) is the magnitude of its velocity vector, v(t) = ‖v(t)‖ = ‖r′(t)‖ = ds/dt, the rate at which the arc length it travels grows.

concepts.name: The plane of the acceleration vector
concepts.statement: The acceleration vector a(t) of an object moving along a curve traced out by a twice-differentiable function r(t) lies in the plane formed by the unit tangent vector T(t) and the principal unit normal vector N(t), the osculating plane, and a(t) = v′(t) T(t) + [v(t)]² κ N(t), where v(t) is the speed and κ the curvature.

concepts.name: Tangential component of acceleration
concepts.statement: The tangential component of acceleration a_T is the coefficient of the unit tangent vector T when the acceleration vector is written as a linear combination of T and N, the projection of a onto T: a_T = a · T = (v · a)/‖v‖.

concepts.name: Normal component of acceleration
concepts.statement: The normal component of acceleration a_N, also called the centripetal or radial component, is the coefficient of the unit normal vector N when the acceleration vector is written as a linear combination of T and N: a_N = a · N = ‖v × a‖/‖v‖ = √(‖a‖² − a_T²).

concepts.name: Projectile motion
concepts.statement: Projectile motion is the motion of an object with an initial velocity but no force acting on it other than gravity, air resistance ignored. Its acceleration is a = −g j, so v(t) = −gt j + v₀ and s(t) = −½gt² j + v₀t + s₀; thrown from the origin at an angle θ with initial speed v₀, s(t) = v₀t cos θ i + (v₀t sin θ − ½gt²) j.

concepts.name: Range of a projectile
concepts.statement: A projectile fired from ground level at an angle θ with initial speed v₀ returns to ground level at t = 2v₀ sin θ/g, a horizontal distance R = v₀² sin 2θ/g; the range is greatest at θ = 45°, where it is v₀²/g.

concepts.name: Kepler’s laws of planetary motion
concepts.statement: The path of any planet about the Sun is elliptical, with the center of the Sun at one focus (the law of ellipses); a line drawn from the center of the Sun to the center of a planet sweeps out equal areas in equal time intervals (the law of equal areas); and the ratio of the squares of the periods of any two planets equals the ratio of the cubes of the lengths of their semimajor axes (the law of harmonies), T_p² = D_p³ with the period in Earth years and the average distance in astronomical units.

concepts.name: Astronomical unit
concepts.statement: One astronomical unit is the average distance from Earth to the Sun, 149,597,870,700 m, or approximately 93,000,000 mi.

concepts.name: An orbit is a conic section
concepts.statement: From Newton’s second law of motion and his law of universal gravitation, F = −(GmM/‖r‖²)(r/‖r‖), the vector r × v is a constant vector C, so the motion lies in a plane perpendicular to C, and ‖r‖ = (‖C‖²/GM)(1/(1 + e cos θ)), with e = ‖D‖/GM: the polar equation of a conic with a focus at the Sun, an ellipse when e < 1.

concepts.name: Kepler’s third law for any two bodies
concepts.statement: For one object of mass m in orbit around another of mass M, such as the Moon around Earth, Kepler’s third law becomes P² = 4π²a³/(G(m + M)), where a is the length of the major axis of the elliptical orbit and P is the period.

concepts.name: Function of two variables
concepts.statement: A function of two variables z = f(x, y) maps each ordered pair (x, y) in a subset D of the real plane ℝ² to a unique real number z. The set D is called the domain of the function, and the range of f is the set of all real numbers z that has at least one ordered pair (x, y) ∈ D such that f(x, y) = z.

concepts.name: Graph of a function of two variables
terms: graph of a function of two variables
concepts.statement: The graph of a function z = f(x, y) of two variables is the set of ordered triples (x, y, z) that satisfies the equation z = f(x, y), plotted in three-dimensional Cartesian space; it is called a surface. A point with positive z lies above the xy-plane and one with negative z below it.

concepts.name: Level curve of a function of two variables
terms: level curve of a function of two variables
concepts.statement: Given a function f(x, y) and a number c in the range of f, a level curve of a function of two variables for the value c is the set of points satisfying the equation f(x, y) = c, completely analogous to a contour line on a topographical map.

concepts.name: Contour map
concepts.statement: A contour map is a graph of the various level curves of a given function f(x, y); where the level curves are obtained for equally spaced values, curves close together mark a steep surface.

concepts.name: Vertical trace
concepts.statement: Consider a function z = f(x, y) with domain D ⊆ ℝ². A vertical trace of the function is either the set of points that solves the equation f(a, y) = z for a given constant x = a, or f(x, b) = z for a given constant y = b; it is graphed in a plane parallel to the yz- or xz-plane.

concepts.name: Functions of more than two variables
concepts.statement: A function of three variables f(x, y, z) maps each point in space to a fourth quantity, such as temperature or wind speed, and a function g(x, y, t) may map a point of the plane to a quantity at a time t. The domain of such a function is found as for one or two variables, from the restrictions that keep its value defined and real.

concepts.name: Level surface of a function of three variables
terms: level surface of a function of three variables
concepts.statement: Given a function f(x, y, z) and a number c in the range of f, a level surface of a function of three variables is the set of points satisfying the equation f(x, y, z) = c.

concepts.name: δ disk
concepts.statement: A δ disk centered at a point (a, b) ∈ ℝ² is the open disk of radius δ centered at (a, b), the set {(x, y) ∈ ℝ² | (x − a)² + (y − b)² < δ²}; it extends the idea of an open interval a − δ < x < a + δ to two variables.

concepts.name: Limit of a function of two variables
concepts.statement: The limit of f(x, y) as (x, y) approaches (a, b) is L, written lim_{(x,y)→(a,b)} f(x, y) = L, if for each ε > 0 there exists a small enough δ > 0 such that for all points (x, y) in a δ disk around (a, b), except possibly for (a, b) itself, the value of f(x, y) is no more than ε away from L: |f(x, y) − L| < ε whenever 0 < √((x − a)² + (y − b)²) < δ.

concepts.name: Limit laws for functions of two variables
concepts.statement: Let f(x, y) and g(x, y) be defined for all (x, y) ≠ (a, b) in a neighborhood around (a, b), with lim f(x, y) = L and lim g(x, y) = M as (x, y) → (a, b), and let c be a constant. Then the limit of a constant is the constant, the limits of x and y are a and b, and the limits of a sum, difference, constant multiple, product, quotient (M ≠ 0), power and root are L + M, L − M, cL, LM, L/M, Lⁿ and ⁿ√L.

concepts.name: A limit must not depend on the path
concepts.statement: Since (a, b) can be approached from an infinite number of directions, the limit of a function of two variables must be the same along every path toward (a, b); if the values of f approach different numbers along two paths, the limit fails to exist.

concepts.name: Interior point
concepts.statement: Let S be a subset of ℝ². A point P₀ is called an interior point of S if there is a δ disk centered around P₀ contained completely in S.

concepts.name: Boundary point
concepts.statement: Let S be a subset of ℝ². A point P₀ is called a boundary point of S if every δ disk centered around P₀ contains points both inside and outside S.

concepts.name: Open set
concepts.statement: A subset S of ℝ² is called an open set if every point of S is an interior point; a δ disk is an example.

concepts.name: Closed set
concepts.statement: A subset S of ℝ² is called a closed set if it contains all its boundary points; a δ disk with its boundary circle included is an example, and a set that contains some but not all of its boundary points is neither open nor closed.

concepts.name: Connected set
concepts.statement: An open set S is a connected set if it cannot be represented as the union of two or more disjoint, nonempty open subsets.

concepts.name: Region
concepts.statement: A set S in ℝ² is a region if it is open, connected and nonempty.

concepts.name: Limit of a function at a boundary point
concepts.statement: Let f be a function of two variables and suppose (a, b) is on the boundary of its domain. The limit of f(x, y) as (x, y) approaches (a, b) is L if for any ε > 0 there exists a δ > 0 such that, for every point (x, y) inside the domain of f and within distance δ of (a, b), |f(x, y) − L| < ε; only the points inside both the δ disk and the domain count.

concepts.name: Continuity of a function of two variables
concepts.statement: A function f(x, y) is continuous at a point (a, b) in its domain if f(a, b) exists, lim_{(x,y)→(a,b)} f(x, y) exists, and lim_{(x,y)→(a,b)} f(x, y) = f(a, b); in terms of ε and δ, |f(x, y) − f(a, b)| < ε whenever √((x − a)² + (y − b)²) < δ.

concepts.name: The sum of continuous functions is continuous
concepts.statement: If f(x, y) is continuous at (x₀, y₀) and g(x, y) is continuous at (x₀, y₀), then f(x, y) + g(x, y) is continuous at (x₀, y₀).

concepts.name: The product of continuous functions is continuous
concepts.statement: If g(x) is continuous at x₀ and h(y) is continuous at y₀, then f(x, y) = g(x)h(y) is continuous at (x₀, y₀).

concepts.name: The composition of continuous functions is continuous
concepts.statement: Let g be a function of two variables from a domain D ⊆ ℝ² to a range R ⊆ ℝ, continuous at (x₀, y₀) ∈ D, and let z₀ = g(x₀, y₀). If f maps ℝ to ℝ and is continuous at z₀, then f ∘ g is continuous at (x₀, y₀).

concepts.name: δ ball
concepts.statement: A δ ball in three dimensions about (x₀, y₀, z₀) consists of all points in ℝ³ lying at a distance of less than δ from it, {(x, y, z) ∈ ℝ³ | √((x − x₀)² + (y − y₀)² + (z − z₀)²) < δ}; a δ ball in more dimensions adds a term under the radical for each. The limit and continuity of a function of three or more variables are defined with δ balls as for two variables with δ disks.

concepts.name: Partial derivative
concepts.statement: Let f(x, y) be a function of two variables. The partial derivative of f with respect to x, written ∂f/∂x or f_x, is ∂f/∂x = lim_{h→0} [f(x + h, y) − f(x, y)]/h, and the partial derivative with respect to y, ∂f/∂y or f_y, is lim_{k→0} [f(x, y + k) − f(x, y)]/k: a derivative of a function of more than one independent variable in which all the variables but one are held constant.

concepts.name: Calculating partial derivatives
concepts.statement: To calculate a partial derivative, treat all independent variables other than the one with respect to which we are differentiating as constants, then differentiate as with a function of a single variable; all the differentiation rules apply.

concepts.name: A partial derivative as a slope
concepts.statement: ∂f/∂x represents the slope of the tangent line passing through the point (x, y, f(x, y)) parallel to the x-axis, the limit of the slopes of secant lines through (x, y, f(x, y)) and (x + h, y, f(x + h, y)), and ∂f/∂y the slope of the tangent line through that point parallel to the y-axis; each is a rate of change of f as we travel parallel to an axis.

concepts.name: Partial derivatives of a function of three variables
concepts.statement: Let f(x, y, z) be a function of three variables. Its partial derivatives with respect to x, y and z are ∂f/∂x = lim_{h→0} [f(x + h, y, z) − f(x, y, z)]/h, ∂f/∂y = lim_{k→0} [f(x, y + k, z) − f(x, y, z)]/k and ∂f/∂z = lim_{m→0} [f(x, y, z + m) − f(x, y, z)]/m, written also f_x, f_y and f_z.

concepts.name: Higher-order partial derivatives
concepts.statement: Each partial derivative of f(x, y) is itself a function of two variables, and its partial derivatives are the second-order partial derivatives ∂²f/∂x², ∂²f/∂x∂y, ∂²f/∂y∂x and ∂²f/∂y² (f_xx, f_yx, f_xy and f_yy), then third-order and so on: second-order or higher partial derivatives, regardless of whether they are mixed.

forms.latex: \frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial x^{2}}=\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left[\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\right],\;\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial x\partial y}=\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left[\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\right],\;\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial y\partial x}=\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left[\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\right],\;\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial y^{2}}=\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left[\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\right]

concepts.name: Mixed partial derivatives
concepts.statement: Higher-order partial derivatives calculated with respect to different variables, such as f_xy and f_yx, are called mixed partial derivatives: at least two of the differentiations are with respect to different variables.

concepts.name: Equality of mixed partial derivatives (Clairaut's theorem)
concepts.statement: Suppose that f(x, y) is defined on an open disk D that contains the point (a, b). If the functions f_xy and f_yx are continuous on D, then f_xy = f_yx: as long as the mixed second-order derivatives are continuous, the order of differentiation does not matter, and the result extends to higher-order derivatives.

concepts.name: Partial differential equation
concepts.statement: A partial differential equation is an equation that involves an unknown function of more than one independent variable and one or more of its partial derivatives.

concepts.name: Heat equation
concepts.statement: The heat equation in two dimensions is u_t = c²(u_xx + u_yy), where the unknown function u(x, y, t) has the spatial variables x and y and the time t and c is a constant; in one dimension it is u_t = c²u_xx, where c² is the thermal diffusivity of the material, and in radial coordinates ∂T/∂t = K[∂²T/∂r² + (2/r) ∂T/∂r].

concepts.name: Wave equation
concepts.statement: The wave equation in two dimensions is u_tt = c²(u_xx + u_yy), where the unknown function u(x, y, t) has the spatial variables x and y and the time t and c is an arbitrary constant.

concepts.name: Laplace's equation
concepts.statement: Laplace's equation in two dimensions is u_xx + u_yy = 0, where the unknown function u has the two independent variables x and y.

concepts.name: A solution of the one-dimensional heat equation
concepts.statement: A solution of u_t = c²u_xx can be written u_m(x, t) = e^{−π²m²c²t} sin(mπx), where m is any positive integer; with m = 1 and initial temperature sin πx over a wire of length 1, the wire cools as time progresses.

concepts.name: Tangent plane
concepts.statement: Let P₀ be a point on a surface S and let C be any curve passing through P₀ and lying entirely in S. If the tangent lines to all such curves C at P₀ lie in the same plane, this plane is the tangent plane to S at P₀. For a surface defined by a differentiable function z = f(x, y), the tangent plane at (x₀, y₀) is z = f(x₀, y₀) + f_x(x₀, y₀)(x − x₀) + f_y(x₀, y₀)(y − y₀), with normal vector f_x(x₀, y₀) i + f_y(x₀, y₀) j − k.

concepts.name: Linear approximation of a function of two variables
concepts.statement: Given a function z = f(x, y) with continuous partial derivatives that exist at the point (x₀, y₀), the linear approximation of f at (x₀, y₀) is L(x, y) = f(x₀, y₀) + f_x(x₀, y₀)(x − x₀) + f_y(x₀, y₀)(y − y₀), the tangent plane to z = f(x, y) at that point; for (x, y) reasonably close to (x₀, y₀) it yields a value reasonably close to f(x, y).

concepts.name: Differentiability of a function of two variables
concepts.statement: A function f(x, y) is differentiable at a point P(x₀, y₀) if, for all points (x, y) in a δ disk around P, f(x, y) = f(x₀, y₀) + f_x(x₀, y₀)(x − x₀) + f_y(x₀, y₀)(y − y₀) + E(x, y), where the error term E satisfies lim E(x, y)/√((x − x₀)² + (y − y₀)²) = 0 as (x, y) → (x₀, y₀): the graph is smooth there, close to its tangent plane near P.

concepts.name: Differentiability implies continuity for functions of two variables
concepts.statement: Let z = f(x, y) be a function of two variables with (x₀, y₀) in its domain. If f(x, y) is differentiable at (x₀, y₀), then f(x, y) is continuous at (x₀, y₀); a function continuous at a point need not be differentiable there.

concepts.name: Continuity of first partials implies differentiability
concepts.statement: Let z = f(x, y) be a function of two variables with (x₀, y₀) in its domain. If f(x, y), f_x(x, y) and f_y(x, y) all exist in a neighborhood of (x₀, y₀) and are continuous at (x₀, y₀), then f(x, y) is differentiable there.

concepts.name: Total differential
concepts.statement: Let z = f(x, y) be differentiable at (x₀, y₀), with differentials dx = Δx and dy = Δy. The differential dz, also called the total differential of z = f(x, y) at (x₀, y₀), is dz = f_x(x₀, y₀) dx + f_y(x₀, y₀) dy; it approximates the change Δz = f(x₀ + Δx, y₀ + Δy) − f(x₀, y₀), so f(x + Δx, y + Δy) ≈ f(x, y) + f_x(x₀, y₀)Δx + f_y(x₀, y₀)Δy, and estimates the propagation of a measurement error.

concepts.name: Differentiability of a function of three variables
concepts.statement: A function f(x, y, z) is differentiable at P(x₀, y₀, z₀) if for all points in a δ ball around P, f(x, y, z) = f(x₀, y₀, z₀) + f_x(x₀, y₀, z₀)(x − x₀) + f_y(x₀, y₀, z₀)(y − y₀) + f_z(x₀, y₀, z₀)(z − z₀) + E(x, y, z), where E(x, y, z)/√((x − x₀)² + (y − y₀)² + (z − z₀)²) → 0; it is then continuous there, and continuity of the first partial derivatives guarantees it.

concepts.name: Chain rule for one independent variable
concepts.statement: Suppose that x = g(t) and y = h(t) are differentiable functions of t and z = f(x, y) is a differentiable function of x and y. Then z = f(x(t), y(t)) is a differentiable function of t and dz/dt = (∂z/∂x)(dx/dt) + (∂z/∂y)(dy/dt), where the ordinary derivatives are evaluated at t and the partial derivatives at (x, y).

concepts.name: Intermediate variable
concepts.statement: Given a composition of functions such as f(x(t), y(t)), the intermediate variables are x and y: they are independent variables for the function f but dependent variables for the variable t.

concepts.name: Tree diagram
concepts.statement: A tree diagram for the chain rule starts at the dependent variable, branches once for each independent variable of the function and again for each variable those depend on, and labels each branch with its derivative; following the branches that end at one variable and adding the products along them gives the chain rule's formula for the derivative with respect to it.

concepts.name: Chain rule for two independent variables
concepts.statement: Suppose x = g(u, v) and y = h(u, v) are differentiable functions of u and v, and z = f(x, y) is a differentiable function of x and y. Then z = f(g(u, v), h(u, v)) is a differentiable function of u and v, and ∂z/∂u = (∂z/∂x)(∂x/∂u) + (∂z/∂y)(∂y/∂u), ∂z/∂v = (∂z/∂x)(∂x/∂v) + (∂z/∂y)(∂y/∂v).

forms.latex: \frac{\partial z}{\partial u}=\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}\frac{\partial x}{\partial u}+\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}\frac{\partial y}{\partial u}
\frac{\partial z}{\partial v}=\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}\frac{\partial x}{\partial v}+\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}\frac{\partial y}{\partial v}

concepts.name: Generalized chain rule
concepts.statement: Let w = f(x₁, x₂, …, x_m) be a differentiable function of m independent variables, and for each i let x_i = x_i(t₁, t₂, …, t_n) be a differentiable function of n independent variables. Then ∂w/∂t_j = (∂w/∂x₁)(∂x₁/∂t_j) + (∂w/∂x₂)(∂x₂/∂t_j) + ⋯ + (∂w/∂x_m)(∂x_m/∂t_j) for any j: the chain rule extended to functions of more than one independent variable.

forms.latex: \frac{\partial w}{\partial t_{j}}=\frac{\partial w}{\partial x_{1}}\frac{\partial x_{1}}{\partial t_{j}}+\frac{\partial w}{\partial x_{2}}\frac{\partial x_{2}}{\partial t_{j}}+\cdots +\frac{\partial w}{\partial x_{m}}\frac{\partial x_{m}}{\partial t_{j}}

concepts.name: Implicit differentiation of a function of two or more variables
concepts.statement: If the equation f(x, y) = 0 defines y implicitly as a function y = g(x) of x, then dy/dx = −(∂f/∂x)/(∂f/∂y), provided f_y(x, y) ≠ 0; if f(x, y, z) = 0 defines z implicitly as a differentiable function of x and y, then ∂z/∂x = −(∂f/∂x)/(∂f/∂z) and ∂z/∂y = −(∂f/∂y)/(∂f/∂z) as long as f_z(x, y, z) ≠ 0. It follows from the chain rule for two independent variables.

forms.latex: \frac{\partial z}{\partial x}=-\frac{\partial f/\partial x}{\partial f/\partial z}\;\text{and}\;\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}=-\frac{\partial f/\partial y}{\partial f/\partial z}

concepts.name: Directional derivative
concepts.statement: Suppose z = f(x, y) is a function of two variables with domain D, let (a, b) ∈ D and u = cos θ i + sin θ j. The directional derivative of f in the direction of u is D_u f(a, b) = lim_{h→0} [f(a + h cos θ, b + h sin θ) − f(a, b)]/h, provided the limit exists: the slope of the tangent line to the surface in the direction of u.

concepts.name: Directional derivative of a function of two variables
concepts.statement: Let z = f(x, y) be differentiable with f_x and f_y existing. Then the directional derivative of f in the direction of u = cos θ i + sin θ j is D_u f(x, y) = f_x(x, y) cos θ + f_y(x, y) sin θ, the dot product ∇f(x, y) · u.

concepts.name: Gradient
concepts.statement: Let z = f(x, y) be a function of x and y such that f_x and f_y exist. The vector ∇f(x, y) = f_x(x, y) i + f_y(x, y) j is called the gradient of f, read "del f" and also written "grad f"; for a nonunit direction vector, dividing by its norm gives the u of the directional derivative.

concepts.name: Properties of the gradient
concepts.statement: Suppose z = f(x, y) is differentiable at (x₀, y₀). If ∇f(x₀, y₀) = 0, then D_u f(x₀, y₀) = 0 for any unit vector u. If ∇f(x₀, y₀) ≠ 0, then D_u f(x₀, y₀) = ‖∇f(x₀, y₀)‖ cos φ is maximized when u points in the same direction as ∇f(x₀, y₀), with maximum value ‖∇f(x₀, y₀)‖, the rate of greatest ascent, and minimized when u points in the opposite direction, with minimum value −‖∇f(x₀, y₀)‖.

concepts.name: Gradient is normal to the level curve
concepts.statement: Suppose z = f(x, y) has continuous first-order partial derivatives in an open disk centered at (x₀, y₀). If ∇f(x₀, y₀) ≠ 0, then ∇f(x₀, y₀) is normal to the level curve of f at (x₀, y₀), since ∇f · ⟨x′(t), y′(t)⟩ = 0 along the level curve; reversing its components and multiplying one by −1 gives a tangent vector.

concepts.name: Gradient of a function of three variables
concepts.statement: Let w = f(x, y, z) be a function of three variables such that f_x, f_y and f_z exist. The vector ∇f(x, y, z) = f_x(x, y, z) i + f_y(x, y, z) j + f_z(x, y, z) k is called the gradient of f, also written grad f(x, y, z).

concepts.name: Directional derivative of a function of three variables
concepts.statement: Suppose w = f(x, y, z) has domain D, (x₀, y₀, z₀) ∈ D, and u = cos α i + cos β j + cos γ k is a unit vector whose components are the directional cosines. The directional derivative of f in the direction of u is D_u f(x₀, y₀, z₀) = lim_{t→0} [f(x₀ + t cos α, y₀ + t cos β, z₀ + t cos γ) − f(x₀, y₀, z₀)]/t, provided the limit exists; for a differentiable f it equals ∇f(x, y, z) · u = f_x cos α + f_y cos β + f_z cos γ.

concepts.name: Critical point of a function of two variables
terms: critical point of a function of two variables
concepts.statement: Let z = f(x, y) be defined on an open set containing (x₀, y₀). The point (x₀, y₀) is a critical point of f if f_x(x₀, y₀) = f_y(x₀, y₀) = 0, or if either f_x(x₀, y₀) or f_y(x₀, y₀) does not exist.

concepts.name: Local and global extrema of a function of two variables
concepts.statement: Let z = f(x, y) be defined and continuous on an open set containing (x₀, y₀). Then f has a local maximum at (x₀, y₀) if f(x₀, y₀) ≥ f(x, y) for all points within some disk centered at (x₀, y₀), and a local minimum if f(x₀, y₀) ≤ f(x, y) there; where the inequality holds for every point of the domain, the maximum or minimum is global (absolute). Either local value is a local extremum.

concepts.name: Fermat's theorem for functions of two variables
concepts.statement: Let z = f(x, y) be defined and continuous on an open set containing (x₀, y₀), and suppose f_x and f_y each exist at (x₀, y₀). If f has a local extremum at (x₀, y₀), then (x₀, y₀) is a critical point of f.

concepts.name: Saddle point
concepts.statement: Given z = f(x, y), the point (x₀, y₀, f(x₀, y₀)) is a saddle point if both f_x(x₀, y₀) = 0 and f_y(x₀, y₀) = 0 but f does not have a local extremum at (x₀, y₀); at the origin of z = x² − y² the surface is a maximum along one trace and a minimum along another.

concepts.name: Discriminant
concepts.statement: The discriminant of f(x, y) at a point (x₀, y₀) where f_x = f_y = 0 is D = f_xx(x₀, y₀) f_yy(x₀, y₀) − (f_xy(x₀, y₀))², which replaces f″(x₀) in the second derivative test.

concepts.name: Second derivative test for functions of two variables
concepts.statement: Let z = f(x, y) have continuous first- and second-order partial derivatives on some disk containing (x₀, y₀), with f_x(x₀, y₀) = f_y(x₀, y₀) = 0, and D its discriminant there. If D > 0 and f_xx(x₀, y₀) > 0, f has a local minimum at (x₀, y₀); if D > 0 and f_xx(x₀, y₀) < 0, a local maximum; if D < 0, a saddle point; if D = 0, the test is inconclusive.

concepts.name: Using the second derivative test for functions of two variables
concepts.statement: Determine the critical points (x₀, y₀) of f where f_x = f_y = 0, discarding any where a partial derivative does not exist; calculate the discriminant D = f_xx f_yy − (f_xy)² at each; and apply the second derivative test to decide whether each is a local maximum, local minimum or saddle point, or whether the test is inconclusive.

concepts.name: Bounded set
concepts.statement: A set is bounded if all the points in that set can be contained within a ball (or disk) of finite radius; a closed, bounded set replaces the closed interval of one variable.

concepts.name: Extreme value theorem for functions of two variables
concepts.statement: A continuous function f(x, y) on a closed and bounded set D in the plane attains an absolute maximum value at some point of D and an absolute minimum value at some point of D.

concepts.name: Finding extreme values of a function of two variables
concepts.statement: If z = f(x, y) is differentiable on a closed, bounded set D, its absolute maximum and minimum values are the largest and smallest values found among the values of f at the critical points of f in D and the values of f on the boundary of D; it follows from the extreme value theorem and Fermat's theorem.

concepts.name: Finding absolute maximum and minimum values
concepts.statement: To find the absolute extrema of a continuous, differentiable f on a closed, bounded set D: determine the critical points of f in D, calculate f at each, determine the maximum and minimum values of f on the boundary (parameterizing its segments or curves, or by Lagrange multipliers), and take the largest and smallest of all these values.

concepts.name: Constraint
concepts.statement: A constraint is an inequality or equation involving one or more variables that is used in an optimization problem; it enforces a limit on the possible solutions, such as the budget 20x + 4y ≤ 216 on golf balls and advertising.

concepts.name: Objective function
concepts.statement: In an optimization problem, the objective function is the function f(x, y) that is to be maximized or minimized subject to the constraints.

concepts.name: Method of Lagrange multipliers: one constraint
concepts.statement: Let f and g be functions of two variables with continuous partial derivatives at every point of some open set containing the smooth curve g(x, y) = 0. If f, restricted to points on the curve g(x, y) = 0, has a local extremum at (x₀, y₀) and ∇g(x₀, y₀) ≠ 0, then there is a number λ, called a Lagrange multiplier, for which ∇f(x₀, y₀) = λ∇g(x₀, y₀): at the extremum the level curve of f is tangent to the constraint and the two gradients are parallel. With three variables the same equations ∇f = λ∇g, g = 0 are solved.

concepts.name: Lagrange multiplier
concepts.statement: A Lagrange multiplier is the constant (or constants) used in the method of Lagrange multipliers; in the case of one constant, it is represented by the variable λ.

concepts.name: Steps for using Lagrange multipliers
concepts.statement: Determine the objective function f(x, y) and the constraint function g(x, y), and whether f is to be maximized or minimized; set up the system ∇f(x₀, y₀) = λ∇g(x₀, y₀), g(x₀, y₀) = 0; solve for x₀ and y₀; the largest of the values of f at the solutions maximizes f and the smallest minimizes it.

concepts.name: Lagrange multipliers with two constraints
concepts.statement: To optimize w = f(x, y, z) subject to two constraints g(x, y, z) = 0 and h(x, y, z) = 0, there are two Lagrange multipliers λ₁ and λ₂, and the system of equations is ∇f(x₀, y₀, z₀) = λ₁∇g(x₀, y₀, z₀) + λ₂∇h(x₀, y₀, z₀), g(x₀, y₀, z₀) = 0, h(x₀, y₀, z₀) = 0.

concepts.name: Double Riemann sum
concepts.statement: Divide the rectangle R = [a, b] × [c, d] into m by n subrectangles R_ij of area ΔA = Δx Δy and choose a sample point (x*_ij, y*_ij) in each; the double Riemann sum ΣΣ f(x*_ij, y*_ij) ΔA adds the volumes of the thin boxes above the R_ij and approximates the volume of the solid above R and under the graph of f.

concepts.name: Double integral
concepts.statement: The double integral of the function f(x, y) over the rectangular region R in the xy-plane is the limit of its double Riemann sums as m and n increase without bound. If f(x, y) ≥ 0, it is the volume V of the solid that lies above R and under the graph of f; if f is ever negative, it is a signed volume.

concepts.name: Integrable function of two variables
concepts.statement: The double integral of f over R exists provided f is not too discontinuous: if f is bounded and continuous over R except on a finite number of smooth curves, the double integral exists and f is integrable over R.

concepts.name: Properties of double integrals
concepts.statement: For f and g integrable over the rectangle R, subregions S and T of R, a constant c and real numbers m and M: the integral of a sum is the sum of the integrals; a constant comes out of the integral; if R = S ∪ T overlapping only on their boundaries, the integral over R is the sum of the integrals over S and T; if f ≥ g on R, the integral of f is at least the integral of g; if m ≤ f ≤ M, then m × A(R) ≤ ∬_R f dA ≤ M × A(R); and if f(x, y) = g(x)h(y), the double integral is the product of the single integrals of g and h.

concepts.name: Iterated integral
concepts.statement: An iterated integral of f(x, y) over the rectangle R = [a, b] × [c, d] integrates with respect to one variable while holding the other constant, then integrates the result with respect to the other: ∫ₐᵇ [∫꜀ᵈ f(x, y) dy] dx or ∫꜀ᵈ [∫ₐᵇ f(x, y) dx] dy.

concepts.name: Fubini's theorem
concepts.statement: If f(x, y) is continuous over a rectangular region R = [a, b] × [c, d], the double integral of f over R equals the iterated integral in either order; more generally this is true if f is bounded on R and discontinuous only on a finite number of continuous curves.

concepts.name: Area of a region by a double integral
concepts.statement: The area of a plane region is the double integral of the constant function 1 over it: A(R) = ∬_R 1 dA for a rectangle R, and A(D) = ∬_D 1 dA for a plane-bounded region D.

concepts.name: Average value of a function of two variables
concepts.statement: The average value of a function of two variables over a region R is its double integral over R divided by the area of R; over a plane-bounded region D of positive area A(D), f_ave = (1/A(D)) ∬_D f(x, y) dA.

concepts.name: Type I region
concepts.statement: A region D in the xy-plane is of Type I if it lies between two vertical lines and the graphs of two continuous functions g₁(x) and g₂(x): D = {(x, y) | a ≤ x ≤ b, g₁(x) ≤ y ≤ g₂(x)}.

forms.latex: D=\{(x,y)\mid a\le x\le b,\;g_{1}(x)\le y\le g_{2}(x)\}

concepts.name: Type II region
concepts.statement: A region D in the xy-plane is of Type II if it lies between two horizontal lines and the graphs of two continuous functions h₁(y) and h₂(y): D = {(x, y) | c ≤ y ≤ d, h₁(y) ≤ x ≤ h₂(y)}.

forms.latex: D=\{(x,y)\mid c\le y\le d,\;h_{1}(y)\le x\le h_{2}(y)\}

concepts.name: Double integral over a nonrectangular region
concepts.statement: If g(x, y) is the extension to a rectangle R of the integrable function f(x, y) defined on a region D inside R, equal to f on D and 0 at every point of R not in D, then g is integrable and the double integral of f over D is the double integral of g over R.

concepts.name: Fubini's theorem (strong form)
concepts.statement: For a function f(x, y) continuous on a region D of Type I, the double integral over D is the iterated integral ∫ₐᵇ [∫_{g₁(x)}^{g₂(x)} f(x, y) dy] dx; on a region of Type II it is ∫꜀ᵈ [∫_{h₁(y)}^{h₂(y)} f(x, y) dx] dy.

concepts.name: Decomposing regions into smaller regions
concepts.statement: If a region D is the union D₁ ∪ D₂ of two regions that do not overlap except at their boundaries, the double integral over D is the sum of the double integrals over D₁ and D₂; a region is often split this way into regions of Type I and Type II.

concepts.name: Changing the order of integration
concepts.statement: To reverse the order of an iterated integral, describe its region the other way, as Type II instead of Type I or the reverse, solving the boundary curves for the other variable and splitting the region where one description needs several pieces; one order may lead to a computation significantly simpler than the other.

concepts.name: Improper double integral
concepts.statement: An improper double integral is an integral ∬_D f dA where either D is an unbounded region or f is an unbounded function.

concepts.name: Fubini's theorem for improper integrals
concepts.statement: If D is a bounded rectangle or simple region described both as {a ≤ x ≤ b, g(x) ≤ y ≤ h(x)} and as {c ≤ y ≤ d, j(y) ≤ x ≤ k(y)}, and f is a nonnegative function on D with finitely many discontinuities in the interior of D, then the improper double integral of f over D equals either iterated integral.

concepts.name: Improper integrals on an unbounded region
concepts.statement: If R is an unbounded rectangle such as {a ≤ x < ∞, c ≤ y < ∞}, then when the limit exists the double integral of f over R is the limit as (b, d) → (∞, ∞) of the iterated integral over [a, b] × [c, d], in either order.

concepts.name: Joint density function
concepts.statement: The joint density function f of a pair of continuous random variables X and Y gives the probability that (X, Y) lies in a region D as the double integral of f over D; since probabilities lie between 0 and 1, f(x, y) ≥ 0 and its integral over the whole plane is 1.

concepts.name: Independent random variables
concepts.statement: The random variables X and Y are independent if their joint density function is the product of their individual density functions, f(x, y) = f₁(x)f₂(y).

concepts.name: Expected value
concepts.statement: The expected values of the random variables X and Y with joint density f over the sample space S are E(X) = ∬_S x f(x, y) dA and E(Y) = ∬_S y f(x, y) dA.

concepts.name: Polar rectangle
concepts.statement: A polar rectangle is the region enclosed between the circles r = a and r = b and the angles θ = α and θ = β, R = {(r, θ) | a ≤ r ≤ b, α ≤ θ ≤ β}; its sides have constant r-values and constant θ-values. A polar subrectangle of sides Δr and Δθ has area ΔA = r* Δr Δθ, r* the average of its radii.

concepts.name: Double integral over a polar rectangular region
concepts.statement: The double integral of f(r, θ) over a polar rectangular region R is the limit of the double Riemann sums ΣΣ f(r*_ij, θ*_ij) r*_ij Δr Δθ of the polar boxes above the polar subrectangles, as m and n increase without bound.

concepts.name: Double integral in polar coordinates
concepts.statement: A double integral over a polar rectangle is the iterated integral ∫_α^β ∫ₐᵇ f(r, θ) r dr dθ: in polar coordinates dA is replaced by r dr dθ, and a function given in x and y changes by x = r cos θ and y = r sin θ.

concepts.name: Double integral over a general polar region
concepts.statement: If f(r, θ) is continuous on a general polar region D = {(r, θ) | α ≤ θ ≤ β, h₁(θ) ≤ r ≤ h₂(θ)}, its double integral over D is ∫_α^β ∫_{h₁(θ)}^{h₂(θ)} f(r, θ) r dr dθ.

concepts.name: Volumes and areas in polar coordinates
concepts.statement: The volume of the solid under z = f(r, θ) above a polar region is ∬ f(r, θ) r dr dθ over that region, and the area of a polar region is the integral of 1 r dr dθ over it.

concepts.name: Triple Riemann sum
concepts.statement: Divide a rectangular box B into l m n subboxes B_ijk of volume ΔV = Δx Δy Δz and choose a sample point in each; the triple Riemann sum is ΣΣΣ f(x*_ijk, y*_ijk, z*_ijk) Δx Δy Δz.

concepts.name: Triple integral
concepts.statement: The triple integral of a function f(x, y, z) over a rectangular box B is the limit of its triple Riemann sums as l, m and n increase without bound, if the limit exists; it exists when f is continuous on B, and f is then integrable on B.

concepts.name: Fubini's theorem for triple integrals
concepts.statement: If f(x, y, z) is continuous on a rectangular box B = [a, b] × [c, d] × [r, s], its triple integral over B equals the iterated integral ∫ᵣˢ ∫꜀ᵈ ∫ₐᵇ f dx dy dz and any of the other five orderings.

concepts.name: Triple integral over a general region
concepts.statement: The triple integral of a continuous function over a general region E = {(x, y, z) | (x, y) ∈ D, u₁(x, y) ≤ z ≤ u₂(x, y)}, where D is the projection of E onto the xy-plane, is the double integral over D of ∫_{u₁}^{u₂} f dz; projections onto the xz- and yz-planes work the same way, and with D of Type I or Type II the integral becomes a threefold iterated integral.

concepts.name: Volume by a triple integral
concepts.statement: The volume of a general solid bounded region E is the triple integral of 1 over E, V(E) = ∭_E 1 dV.

concepts.name: Average value of a function of three variables
concepts.statement: If f(x, y, z) is integrable over a solid bounded region E with positive volume V(E), its average value is its triple integral over E divided by V(E).

concepts.name: Triple integral in cylindrical coordinates
concepts.statement: Over a cylindrical box B = {(r, θ, z) | a ≤ r ≤ b, α ≤ θ ≤ β, c ≤ z ≤ d}, the triple integral in cylindrical coordinates is the limit of the triple Riemann sums ΣΣΣ f(r*, θ*, z*) r* Δr Δθ Δz; a function g(x, y, z) given in rectangular coordinates is integrated as g(r cos θ, r sin θ, z) r dr dθ dz.

concepts.name: Fubini's theorem in cylindrical coordinates
concepts.statement: If g(x, y, z) is continuous on a portion of a circular cylinder B = {(r, θ, z) | a ≤ r ≤ b, α ≤ θ ≤ β, c ≤ z ≤ d}, its triple integral is ∫꜀ᵈ ∫_α^β ∫ₐᵇ f(r, θ, z) r dr dθ dz with f(r, θ, z) = g(r cos θ, r sin θ, z), or any of the other five orders. Over a general region E between z = u₁(r, θ) and z = u₂(r, θ) above its projection D, the inner integral runs from u₁ to u₂.

concepts.name: Volume element in spherical coordinates
concepts.statement: A spherical subbox with sides Δρ, ρΔφ and ρ sin φ Δθ has volume ΔV = (Δρ)(ρ Δφ)(ρ sin φ Δθ) = ρ² sin φ Δρ Δφ Δθ.

concepts.name: Triple integral in spherical coordinates
concepts.statement: The triple integral in spherical coordinates over a spherical box B = {(ρ, θ, φ) | a ≤ ρ ≤ b, α ≤ θ ≤ β, γ ≤ φ ≤ ψ} is the limit of the triple Riemann sums ΣΣΣ f(ρ*, θ*, φ*)(ρ*)² sin φ* Δρ Δθ Δφ, provided the limit exists.

concepts.name: Fubini's theorem for spherical coordinates
concepts.statement: If f(ρ, θ, φ) is continuous on a spherical solid box B = [a, b] × [α, β] × [γ, ψ], its triple integral is the iterated integral ∫_α^β ∫_γ^ψ ∫ₐᵇ f ρ² sin φ dρ dφ dθ, or any other order; over a general region with φ between u₁(ρ, θ) and u₂(ρ, θ) the inner integral runs between them.

concepts.name: Density of a lamina
concepts.statement: The density ρ(x, y) of a lamina at a point is the limit of Δm/ΔA, the mass per area of a small rectangle containing the point, as the dimensions of the rectangle go to 0; it is measured in units of mass per unit area.

concepts.name: Mass of a lamina
concepts.statement: The mass of a lamina occupying a region R with density ρ(x, y) is the limit of the sums of the masses ρ(x*_ij, y*_ij) ΔA of its subrectangles, the double integral of ρ over R.

concepts.name: Moments of a lamina
concepts.statement: The moment M_x of a lamina about the x-axis is the double integral of yρ(x, y) over its region, and its moment M_y about the y-axis is the double integral of xρ(x, y).

concepts.name: Center of mass of a lamina
concepts.statement: The center of mass of a lamina is the point (x̄, ȳ) with x̄ = M_y/m and ȳ = M_x/m, each a quotient of double integrals; the lamina balances on it.

concepts.name: Centroid of a plane region
concepts.statement: For a constant density the density cancels and the center of mass coincides with the centroid of the region: x_c = ∬_R x dA / ∬_R dA and y_c = ∬_R y dA / ∬_R dA.

concepts.name: Moments of inertia of a lamina
concepts.statement: The moment of inertia of a particle of mass m about an axis is mr², r its distance from the axis; the moments of inertia of a lamina about the x-axis and the y-axis are I_x = ∬_R y²ρ(x, y) dA and I_y = ∬_R x²ρ(x, y) dA. A moment of inertia measures the tendency of the mass to resist a change in rotational motion about an axis.

concepts.name: Polar moment of inertia
concepts.statement: The polar moment of inertia I₀ of a lamina, its moment of inertia about the origin, is I_x + I_y, the double integral of (x² + y²)ρ(x, y).

concepts.name: Radius of gyration
concepts.statement: The radius of gyration of an object about an axis is the distance from the axis at which its whole mass might be concentrated to give the same moment of inertia: R_x = √(I_x/m), R_y = √(I_y/m) and R₀ = √(I₀/m).

concepts.name: Mass and moments of a solid
concepts.statement: A solid object Q with density ρ(x, y, z) has mass m = ∭_Q ρ dV and moments M_xy, M_xz and M_yz about the xy-, xz- and yz-planes, the triple integrals of zρ, yρ and xρ.

concepts.name: Center of mass of a solid
concepts.statement: The center of mass of a solid is the point (x̄, ȳ, z̄) with x̄ = M_yz/m, ȳ = M_xz/m and z̄ = M_xy/m; for a homogeneous solid, of constant density, it is the centroid of the solid.

concepts.name: Moments of inertia of a solid
concepts.statement: The moments of inertia of a solid Q of density ρ are I_x = ∭_Q (y² + z²)ρ dV, I_y = ∭_Q (x² + z²)ρ dV and I_z = ∭_Q (x² + y²)ρ dV.

concepts.name: Transformation
concepts.statement: A transformation, or mapping, is the function used to change the variables of an integral to make the integration simpler, as x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ changes a double integral to polar coordinates.

concepts.name: Planar transformation
concepts.statement: A planar transformation T is a function that transforms a region G in one plane into a region R in another plane by a change of variables x = g(u, v), y = h(u, v); G is the domain of T and R, its range, is the image of G under T.

concepts.name: One-to-one transformation
concepts.statement: A transformation T: G → R, T(u, v) = (x, y), is one-to-one if no two points map to the same image point; then its inverse T⁻¹ exists with domain R.

concepts.name: C¹ transformation
concepts.statement: A transformation T(u, v) = (g(u, v), h(u, v)) is a C¹ transformation if its component functions have continuous first partial derivatives g_u, g_v, h_u and h_v.

concepts.name: Jacobian
concepts.statement: The Jacobian of the C¹ transformation T(u, v) = (g(u, v), h(u, v)) is the 2 × 2 determinant J(u, v) = ∂(x, y)/∂(u, v) = x_u y_v − x_v y_u; a small rectangle Δu by Δv is carried to a region of area ΔA ≈ J(u, v) Δu Δv, the area of the parallelogram of Δu r_u and Δv r_v.

forms.latex: J(u,v)=\left|\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|=\begin{vmatrix}\frac{\partial x}{\partial u}&\frac{\partial y}{\partial u}\\\frac{\partial x}{\partial v}&\frac{\partial y}{\partial v}\end{vmatrix}=\frac{\partial x}{\partial u}\frac{\partial y}{\partial v}-\frac{\partial x}{\partial v}\frac{\partial y}{\partial u}

concepts.name: Change of variables for double integrals
concepts.statement: If T(u, v) = (x, y), x = g(u, v), y = h(u, v), is a one-to-one C¹ transformation with a nonzero Jacobian on the interior of a region S of the uv-plane, mapping S onto R, and f is continuous on R, then ∬_R f(x, y) dA = ∬_S f(g(u, v), h(u, v)) |∂(x, y)/∂(u, v)| du dv: dA is replaced by |J| du dv.

concepts.name: Changing variables in a multiple integral
concepts.statement: To change variables: sketch the region in the xy-plane and write the equations of its boundary curves; choose the transformation x = g(u, v), y = h(u, v) from the region or the integrand; determine the new limits of integration in the uv-plane; find the Jacobian J(u, v); replace the variables in the integrand; and replace dy dx or dx dy by J(u, v) du dv.

concepts.name: Jacobian in three variables
concepts.statement: The Jacobian J(u, v, w) = ∂(x, y, z)/∂(u, v, w) of a transformation x = g(u, v, w), y = h(u, v, w), z = k(u, v, w) is the 3 × 3 determinant of its first partial derivatives.

forms.latex: J(u,v,w)=\begin{vmatrix}\frac{\partial x}{\partial u}&\frac{\partial x}{\partial v}&\frac{\partial x}{\partial w}\\\frac{\partial y}{\partial u}&\frac{\partial y}{\partial v}&\frac{\partial y}{\partial w}\\\frac{\partial z}{\partial u}&\frac{\partial z}{\partial v}&\frac{\partial z}{\partial w}\end{vmatrix}

concepts.name: Change of variables for triple integrals
concepts.statement: If T(u, v, w) = (x, y, z) is a one-to-one C¹ transformation with a nonzero Jacobian mapping a region G of uvw-space onto R in xyz-space, and F is continuous on R, then ∭_R F dV = ∭_G F(g, h, k) |∂(x, y, z)/∂(u, v, w)| du dv dw; cylindrical and spherical coordinates are the cases |J| = r and |J| = ρ² sin φ.

concepts.name: Vector field
concepts.statement: A vector field F in ℝ² is an assignment of a two-dimensional vector F(x, y) to each point (x, y) of a subset D of ℝ², the domain of the vector field; a vector field in ℝ³ assigns a three-dimensional vector F(x, y, z) to each point (x, y, z) of a subset D of ℝ³. It is written with component functions, F(x, y) = ⟨P(x, y), Q(x, y)⟩ = P i + Q j, or F(x, y, z) = ⟨P, Q, R⟩ = P i + Q j + R k, and it is continuous if its component functions are continuous.

concepts.name: Radial field
concepts.statement: In a radial field, all vectors either point directly toward or directly away from the origin, and the magnitude of any vector depends only on its distance from the origin; the vector at (x, y) is perpendicular to the circle centered at the origin through (x, y).

concepts.name: Rotational field
concepts.statement: In a rotational field, the vector at point (x, y) is tangent to the circle with radius r = √(x² + y²); in a standard rotational field all vectors point clockwise or all counterclockwise, and the magnitude of a vector depends only on its distance from the origin.

concepts.name: Unit vector field
concepts.statement: A vector field F is a unit vector field if the magnitude of each vector in the field is 1; dividing F by its magnitude to form the unit vector field F/‖F‖ = ⟨P/‖F‖, Q/‖F‖, R/‖F‖⟩ is called normalizing F.

concepts.name: Conservative vector field
concepts.statement: A vector field F in ℝ² or in ℝ³ is a gradient field, or conservative field, if there exists a scalar function f such that ∇f = F; such fields model physical systems in which energy is conserved.

concepts.name: Potential function
concepts.statement: If F is a conservative vector field, a scalar function f such that ∇f = F is called a potential function for F.

concepts.name: Uniqueness of potential functions
concepts.statement: Let F be a conservative vector field on an open and connected domain and let f and g be functions such that ∇f = F and ∇g = F. Then there is a constant C such that f = g + C.

concepts.name: Cross-partial property of conservative vector fields
concepts.statement: Let F be a vector field whose component functions have continuous first-order partial derivatives. If F = ⟨P, Q⟩ is conservative in ℝ², then ∂P/∂y = ∂Q/∂x; if F = ⟨P, Q, R⟩ is conservative in ℝ³, then ∂P/∂y = ∂Q/∂x, ∂Q/∂z = ∂R/∂y and ∂R/∂x = ∂P/∂z. The converse does not follow, so the property shows a field is not conservative but cannot show that it is.

forms.latex: \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}=\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x},\;\frac{\partial Q}{\partial z}=\frac{\partial R}{\partial y},\;\frac{\partial R}{\partial x}=\frac{\partial P}{\partial z}

concepts.name: Line integral
concepts.statement: A line integral is the integral of a function along a curve in a plane or in space: a scalar line integral integrates a scalar function, and a vector line integral a vector field.

concepts.name: Scalar line integral
concepts.statement: Let f be a function with a domain that includes the smooth curve C parameterized by r(t), a ≤ t ≤ b. Chop C into n pieces of lengths Δsᵢ and choose a point Pᵢ* in each; the scalar line integral of f along C is the limit of the sums Σ f(Pᵢ*) Δsᵢ as n → ∞, if it exists. If f ≥ 0, it is the area of the sheet dropped from the curve on the graph of f down to C, and it does not depend on the parameterization.

concepts.name: Scalar line integral calculation
concepts.statement: Let f be a continuous function with a domain that includes the smooth curve C with parameterization r(t) = ⟨x(t), y(t), z(t)⟩, a ≤ t ≤ b. Then ∫_C f ds = ∫ₐᵇ f(r(t)) ‖r′(t)‖ dt, so ds = ‖r′(t)‖ dt.

concepts.name: Arc length as a line integral
concepts.statement: If f(x, y, z) = 1, the scalar line integral ∫_C 1 ds is the arc length of C.

concepts.name: Orientation of a curve
concepts.statement: An orientation of a curve C is a specified direction along it, its positive direction, the opposite being the negative direction; an oriented curve is a curve with an orientation, and −C is the same curve with the opposite orientation.

concepts.name: Closed curve
concepts.statement: A closed curve is one for which there exists a parameterization r(t), a ≤ t ≤ b, such that r(a) = r(b) and the curve is traversed exactly once: it begins and ends at the same point.

concepts.name: Vector line integral
concepts.statement: The vector line integral of a vector field F along an oriented smooth curve C is the integral of the dot product of F with the unit tangent vector T of C with respect to arc length, the limit of the sums Σ F(Pᵢ*) · T(Pᵢ*) Δsᵢ, if it exists; it is written ∫_C F · dr and is computed from a parameterization as ∫ₐᵇ F(r(t)) · r′(t) dt, or in the form ∫_C P dx + Q dy + R dz.

concepts.name: Work done by a force field
concepts.statement: The work done by a force field F in moving a particle in the positive direction along an oriented curve C is the vector line integral W = ∫_C F · T ds.

concepts.name: Piecewise smooth curve
concepts.statement: A piecewise smooth curve is an oriented curve that is not smooth but can be written as the union C = C₁ + C₂ + ⋯ + Cₙ of finitely many smooth curves, the endpoint of each the starting point of the next.

concepts.name: Properties of vector line integrals
concepts.statement: For continuous vector fields F and G whose domains include the oriented smooth curve C and a constant k: the line integral of F + G is the sum of the line integrals; ∫_C kF · dr = k ∫_C F · dr; reversing the orientation changes the sign, ∫_{−C} F · dr = −∫_C F · dr; and over a piecewise smooth curve C = C₁ + ⋯ + Cₙ the line integral is the sum of the line integrals over the pieces.

concepts.name: Mass of a wire
concepts.statement: If a thin wire has the shape of a curve C and density ρ(x, y, z) per unit length, its mass is the scalar line integral m = ∫_C ρ(x, y, z) ds.

concepts.name: Flux across a curve
concepts.statement: The flux of a vector field F across a plane curve C, the rate at which a fluid flows across C, is the line integral ∫_C F · (n(t)/‖n(t)‖) ds of the normal component of F; for r(t) = ⟨x(t), y(t)⟩, a ≤ t ≤ b, and n(t) = ⟨y′(t), −x′(t)⟩ it is ∫_C F · N ds = ∫ₐᵇ F(r(t)) · n(t) dt.

concepts.name: Circulation
concepts.statement: The circulation of a vector field F along an oriented closed curve C is the line integral ∮_C F · T ds, the tendency of a fluid to move in the direction of C.

concepts.name: Simple curve
concepts.statement: A curve C is simple if it does not cross itself: there is a parameterization r(t), a ≤ t ≤ b, that is one-to-one over (a, b). A simple curve may also be closed, with r(a) = r(b).

concepts.name: Connected region
concepts.statement: A region D is connected if, for any two points P₁ and P₂ in it, there is a path from P₁ to P₂ with a trace contained entirely inside D.

concepts.name: Simply connected region
concepts.statement: A region D is simply connected if it is connected and any simple closed curve C inside D can be shrunk continuously to a point while staying entirely inside D; in two dimensions, a connected region with no holes.

concepts.name: Fundamental Theorem for Line Integrals
concepts.statement: Let C be a piecewise smooth curve with parameterization r(t), a ≤ t ≤ b, and let f be a function of two or three variables with continuous first-order partial derivatives on C. Then the line integral of ∇f along C depends only on the values of f at the endpoints: ∫_C ∇f · dr = f(r(b)) − f(r(a)).

concepts.name: Path independence
concepts.statement: A vector field F with domain D is independent of path (path independent) if ∫_{C₁} F · dr = ∫_{C₂} F · dr for any paths C₁ and C₂ in D with the same initial and terminal points.

concepts.name: Path independence of conservative fields
concepts.statement: If F is a conservative vector field, then F is independent of path; in particular the circulation of a conservative field around any closed curve is zero.

concepts.name: Path independence test for conservative fields
concepts.statement: If F is a continuous vector field that is independent of path and the domain D of F is open and connected, then F is conservative.

concepts.name: Finding a potential function
concepts.statement: To find a potential function for a conservative field F = ⟨P, Q⟩: integrate P with respect to x to get g(x, y) + h(y) with h unknown; take the partial derivative with respect to y; use g_y(x, y) + h′(y) = Q(x, y) to find h′(y); integrate h′(y) to find h(y); then f(x, y) = g(x, y) + h(y) + C for any constant C. In space the same steps add one more unknown function.

concepts.name: Cross-partial test for conservative fields
concepts.statement: If F = ⟨P, Q, R⟩ is a vector field on an open, simply connected region D, then P_y = Q_x, P_z = R_x and Q_z = R_y throughout D if and only if F is conservative (in two dimensions, P_y = Q_x).

concepts.name: Green's theorem, circulation form
concepts.statement: Green's theorem relates an integral over a region to an integral over its boundary.
